text: 03/08/22, 14:56 rt, U.S. 11::)BANK Interview of Ingrida simonyt, Deputy Chairman of the Governorship of the Bank of Lithuania, to Lithuaniaradias, 081/10/2014 Bank of Lithuania Lietuvosbankovaldybospirminkopavaduotojos Ingridossimonyts interviuLietuvosradijui,2014 10 08 2014-10-29 Ingrida simonyt, Deputy Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, is interviewed by Alvyda Bajarunait. The interview was broadcast on October 8, 2014 at the LRTradijolaide "Morning Sounds". - Why do other countries not adopt the euro, while Lithuania needs it? - Well, those other countries are not only other, but also different, than that there is Lithuania. Most often in discussions examples are our neighbour Poland, as well as Sweden, the United Kingdom. The question is raised yes - why are these countries not in a hurry to join the euro Area? Without a doubt, they have a very weighty for this reason - their monetary policy is simply completely different. Those countries live in free-floating currencies m, from, under the conditions and under those conditions, it is quite beneficial for them not to join the euro area, let alone to do so, that Britain's relationship with the EU is now quite complicated overall, so the euro is here last thing. And Lithuania, twenty years ago, had chosen to record its exchange rate, i.e. in our lives there are a situation where you can wake up in the morning and see that the price of your money is quite different from what it was yesterday, higher or lower, simply because the market has set a different price for the currency. This uncertainty in our life is extinct, because we have fixed our currency to the base currency - initially to the dollar, now to the euro. I have no doubt that you would ask the wives on the street if they would like a free-floating lito, perhaps the vast majority of them would certainly not be fascinated by such a thought. And I'm afraid that in that case, by now, we'd still have everything counting in dollars, as we did 24 years ago. 1/3 03/08/22, 14:56 Interview of Ingrida simonyt, Deputy Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, to Lithuanian Radio, 081/10/2014 Bank of Lithuania So, without a doubt, our calculations are somewhat different. We have a fixed course, we're not going to do that course change, we are not going to let the litas float freely. Then the question arises - and why do we have to pay a supplement for this, that we have a theoretical possibility of devaluing the litas? That supplement, depending on the economic situation, is still there. Today it is very small, because no one expects such an event. But in 2008-2009, if anyone remembers, he was very big. Just for having the opportunity to do something we never did, we had to pay huge interest premiums. - Why was the eurozone created and how much did it work out? Is it possible to generalize today? - It's actually a very long story [...]. The aim was to achieve an increasingly deep integration of EU countries. At first, all this began with the free trade area, later integration deepened. Well, and such a crown of integration would be a common currency and currency union. There is no doubt that this currency union, this euro area, where monetary policy is centralised and budgetary, structural policies are autonomous, has its drawbacks in each country, and any economist would say so, because a currency union is not really optimal. However, you need to understand a little bit of another the momentum that exists in the EU, i.e. namely the [momentum] of deeper integration, of the creation of a stronger core. Therefore, it is precisely precisely political objectives, of course, accompany the euro area as a project. - Eurosceptics often cite the example of Poland. here the Poles do not have the euro, they do not promise to adopt it. What is the difference between Poland's economic situation that it does not need the euro? - [...] We have to come back to what I said at the beginning: Poland's monetary policy is completely different from Lithuania's monetary policy. The zloty is a free-floating currency, the price of a zloty every day, in simple terms, is set by the market. When we talk about how successfully Poland survived the crisis of 2009, [...] as if without loss, we should remember that many people in a neighbouring country liked to go shopping. And certainly not because of lower VAT, but because the zloty was cheaper against the euro and, accordingly, the litas (at the very lowest point - probably about 40%). Such changes are not without loss. Someone still suffers losses in society: whether people who took out loans in currency or those who have savings. But the Polish economy benefited from such fluctuations, as imports became more expensive and exports became cheaper. In this way, Poland has managed to bring the situation under control. But Poland is a large and rather closed economy, so its calculations in this case are different from Lithuania's, which is a small, open economy, which is affected by the winds of imports and exports, for which ensuring the stability of import and export prices is one of the main and most important things. And we achieved this with the Currency Board. If we had not had a Currency Board, I have no doubt, in 2008-2009 the litas would probably have fallen not by 40%, but by much more. This can be thought of by people who have savings, who have loans, say, in euros - how would they have felt at that time? Thus, each calculation in this situation is different. And the calculations of Poland, of course, are different. ko-board-chairman-pava givers-ingridos-simonytes-interview-lithuanian-radio-2014-10-08 2/3 03/08/22, 14:56 Lietuvosbanko valdybospirmininkopavaduotojosIngridossimonyts interviuLietuvosradijui,2014 10 081 Lietuvosbankas But what I would like to pay attention to - this spring, when we were faced with the situation in Eastern Europe - hybrid wars, examples of aggression, even in the rhetoric of Polish politicians and the Central Bank, one can see changes and more open languages. The United Kingdom is another example. Could you comment on it? - Sure. Britain's relationship with the EU - especially at the moment - is generally significantly complicated. I believe that the issue of the euro is already completely secondary. We are hearing about the referendum that the Conservative Government is going to initiate, about the fact that there is a general desire to rethink relations with the EU and to pluck greater benefits for ourselves from it. Title: Interview to the daily newspaper Kauno diena
text: 03/08/22, 14:56 Ingrida simonyt, Deputy Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, interviewed the daily newspaper. Kaunas Day", 2014 11 031 Lithuanian ban... rt, U.S. 11::)BANK Ingrida simonyt, the deputyman of the Chairman of the Lithuanian Bank's Management, to the daily newspaper Kaunodiena, 20141103 2014-11-04 Ingrida simonyt, Deputy Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, is interviewed by Ruta Grigolyt. The interview was published on 3 November 2014 in the daily newspapers "Kaunodiena",,,Klaipeda" and on the portal diena.It. - What do banks operating in Lithuania look like in the context of the euro-zone? Are they quite strong, meet all the requirements? - Lithuanian banks look really good. European The Central Bank (ECB) together with the national comprehensive documentation of the euro area by supervisors an assessment of banks, the conclusions of which have just been published, showed that the three major Lithuanian banks, the supervision of which will be directly responsible from 1 January SI 1 of 1 The ECB stands out in the euro area banking circle with extremely high capital, which has not been reduced by the in-depth wealth carried out. quality assessment. The stress test also revealed that even after assessing the losses, which could be due to a combination of various adverse factors, banks' capital would remain significantly higher than the limit set. Although the smaller banks of the country did not participate in this exercise, the Bank of Lithuania (Bank of Lithuania) constantly monitors their compliance with the established mandatory norms, as well as conducts stress tests in order to assess the resilience of the Lithuanian banking system to shocks. All our banks undoubtedly meet all the capital adequacy and other requirements, and the banking system is resilient to shocks that can be caused by adverse scenarios. It should also be borne in mind that unfavorable scenarios in such tests are hypothetical - this is not some kind of forecast for the future, it is simply an effort to create a "cocktail" of unfavorable circumstances and assess what consequences this would have for the banking system. - What will the monitoring of the Joint Supervisory Mechanism{8PM mean to the three largest banks in Lithuania, or what will they mean - 03/08/22, 14:56 Ingrida simonyt, Deputy Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, interview with the daily newspaper Kauno diena, 031.11.2014 Lithuanian ban ... will have to change something a little bit, reorganize it? Whichit will be the banks? - The ECB will be directly responsible for the supervision of the three major Lithuanian banks - SEB, 11Swedbank11 and DNB - from 1 January. Although our three big banks occupy about 70 prae. in our banking system, in the entire group of banks taken over by the ECB under the direct supervision of the ECB, they are small, not even comparable to the giants 11BNP Paribas11 or 11Deutche Bank11); Risk-based supervision dictates that the ECB's direct attention should be focused on the largest institutions, but how the processes will look in practice and the load on whom will be - it is difficult to say for the time being, because there is no experience. We will see more when the SSM becomes operational, at which point the principles of planning and coordinating work will be clearer. The major Banks of Lithuania will simply have to accept that the final decisions related to them will no longer be taken by the Bank of Lithuania, but by the ECB. They will have to cooperate constructively with the new supervisory authority. - Why are only three banks selected for supervision, and not all banks registered in the country? - These are the provisions of EU law that determine which banks go under the direct supervision of the ECB. It is true that the ECB could at any time also take over any other bank operating in Lithuania under its direct supervision if it saw one Need. - Which section of the financial institutions sector is currently the weakest in Lithuania and for what reasons? - I wouldn't want to stick labels with negative connotations for any particular part of the financial sector, because we have some great examples of activity everywhere. However, a number of bankruptcies have affected credit unions and it cannot be said that this is due to the reasons associated with the regulation and activities of this sector. Although the ominously unsustainable growth of the credit union sector, which has been going on for some time, has stopped with the tightening of capital adequacy requirements by the Bank of Lithuania, it is clear that in order to give credit unions a new breath, a complex reform of the sector is necessary, which solves fundamental problems and allows it to develop in a sustainable way. The Bank of Lithuania has already prepared complex proposals, a working group has been set up in the Seimas to prepare the guidelines for such a reform, so we hope to find a consensus among all interested parties on the issues to be resolved. - Are there currently concerns in the Lithuanian financial sector that need to be urgently corrected? - Concerns remain about the evolution of the consumer credit market. In order to solve the problems arising from irresponsible borrowing and lending, we have submitted proposals for amending the Law on Consumer Credit. The Seimas has set up a special working group to study this issue, where we hope to present our proposals and find laws for them publisher support. ... 03/08/22, 14:56 Interview of Ingrida simonyt, deputyman of the Chairman of the Lithuanian Bank's Management, to the daily newspaper "Kaunodiena", 031.11.2014 Lietuvosban... - How can one assess the overall state of the banking system operating in the euro area? - After the presentation of the results of the comprehensive assessment, it can be seen that the mystical "hole" in the balance sheets of the euro area, which the pessimists talked about, is certainly not large, and there are only a dozen banks that urgently need capital-strengthening measures. Of course, those who want to doubt the result will always find reasons for this, but it should be mentioned that the detailed assessment was carried out very thoroughly, the banks' balance sheets were first examined in detail before applying the stress test, so this is certainly an unprecedented process. Of course, there is still work to be done to strengthen the banking system in the euro area, but this has been done for some time. Since the beginning of the year alone, banks have covered more than half of the capital shortfall identified in the comprehensive assessment. The capital shortfall was assessed on 31 December 2013. - KokiaLietuvaibusnaudais dalyvavimoBPM? - The SSM is designed as a tool to ensure uniform supervisory standards in all euro area countries, eliminating the possibilities to operate in different competitive conditions due to the regulatory arbitrage of national supervisors. As the result of the comprehensive assessment shows, the supervision of the Bank of Lithuania has been really effective, no adjustments have been made to our banks, and in the future the ECB is committed to being a top-level supervisor. - Is it difficult for Lithuania to participate in it? What obligations will the country have? - As I said, it is difficult to discuss for the time being, because the mechanism itself will not be operational until 4 November, and we will join it from 1 January. However, I do not think that there will be special difficulties: the majority of banks operating in Lithuania have major and "sister" companies in other countries, cooperation with other supervisory authorities is common in our work. Banks will have financial obligations - to pay supervisory contributions to the ECB, and the Bank of Lithuania will have to devote its resources to working together with the ECB. - Which euro area countries and which banks are the most problematic, are worried and for what reasons? - A comprehensive assessment revealed which banks lacked the capital to withstand the effects of adverse scenarios. One of the oldest banks is most missing - the Italian Mante dei Paschi di Siena. Banks that still face capital shortages will have to submit capital strengthening plans and take action within 6-9 months to close the hole identified in the comprehensive assessment. The aim of the comprehensive assessment is not only for the ECB to ascertain the state of the banks it is taking over directly, but also to restore confidence in the euro area banking system. This is an important, though not the only, circumstance in anticipation of a recovery in the euro area's struggling economy.

Interviewpublished on January 26, 2015 portale1Smin.lt - The ECB will buy euro area sovereign bonds up to 1.3 trillion. Euro. The ECB reported that the money securities will mainly be bought by the NCBs. What doesit meanfor Lithuaniato becomea fullfledgedmemberof the euroarea andthe Single SupervisoryMechanism{SSM)?How do youfeel aboutjoiningthe SupervisoryBoardas a member? Becoming a full-fledged member of the euro area as m,of 1 soon as possible has always been considered one of the major milestones of our European integration, given that we've been operating currency board arrangements since 1994 and that the litas has been pegged to the euro since February 2002 . In such circumstances, the objective of a prompt membership in the euro area is a natural strategy, especially as our country has undertaken such great efforts to sustain the peg to the euro during the crisis of 2008-09 . Membership in the euro area means the full elimination of foreign exchange risk and transaction costs, and an even more resilient banking sector. It is fortunate that we are joining the Single Supervisory Mechanism and the Supervisory Board almost from the very outset, as there will be less need to adapt and adjust than would otherwise be the case. I am looking forward to working together with my fellow members in order to carry out the tasks for which the SSM has been created. The comprehensiveassessmentwas a previewfor direct ECBsupervisionof the three largestLithuanian banks.How arethe bankspreparedfor the changeover?Whatwas yourrole in this process? https ://www .lb.lt/en/speeches-interviews-presentations/ingrida-simonyte-interview-with-bankingsupervisioneuropa 1eu 1/3 03/08/22, 14:42 lngridaSimonyte:interviewwithSingleSupervisoryMechanismofficialwebsitebankingsupervision.europa.eIuBankof Lithuania Two of the largest have their sister banks in Estonia and Latvia, so it was a horizontal exercise for them and the group of SEB and Swedbank, despite the fact that, as a group, they do not fall under the umbrella of the Single Supervisory Mechanism. The third bank - DNB - also participated in the exercise in Estonia. There was scope for synergies in many respects. The banks did well and corrections were minor, even under the stress scenario. In any event, capital remained well above the minima. This represents the fact that they all took a very prudent stance after the global crisis had hit, recognising potential losses under very conservative assumptions, so that there was no real need for any adjustments at this time. I have no doubt that we are joining the SSM from a very sustainable base. The Bank of Lithuania played a very extensive role in the process, given that we had less time for the exercise than other countries, since we started later. Therefore, we were involved not only in coordinating and supervising. We also performed some parts of the asset quality review in order to deliver on time and to have a cost-effective exercise, since it was challenging for local auditors and consultants to provide enough staff at such short notice. Whatare the mainfeaturesof Lithuania'sbankingsectorandwhat impactwill ECBsupervisionhave? As I have already mentioned, the pattern of the banking system is similar to that of the other Baltic countries, as even the names of major banks are largely the same. The banking system is dominated by subsidiaries of Nordic banks, with three major banks accounting for approximately 70% of the market share. There are a few smaller banks that will not fall under the definition of systemically important institutions, and some branches. The banking system showed resilience during the crisis, as losses were in most cases recognised immediately, and capital has been strengthened. Some small banks, however, had to be wound down in 2011-13, because of mismanagement, but that had no systemic negative spillover, and the overall banking system became even more resilient and prudent. The prudential ratios of banks operating in Lithuania continue to significantly exceed the required minimum amounts. For example, on 1 October 2014, the banking system's capital adequacy ratio was 20.7%. Lithuania'sthree significant banks are all subsidiaries of foreign banking groups that have their headquartersin non-participatingcountries.How will cooperationwith the home supervisorsof these banksworkunderthe SSM? Cooperation between the Bank of Lithuania and the consolidating supervisors of the three largest banks, which are located in Sweden and Norway, has long been in place and serves as a good example of crossborder supervision. The supervisory colleges have ensured an efficient and well-organised dialogue between 2/3 03/08/22, 14:42 lngridaSimonyte:interviewwithSingleSupervisoryMechanismofficialwebsitebankingsupervision.europa.eIuBankof Lithuania the national supervisory authorities, and certainly serve their purpose. Under the SSM,the ECBwill become a full-fledged member of these colleges, continuing and contributing to the productive experience. National supervisors from participating countries, including the Bank of Lithuania, will remain in supervisory colleges as observers and will fully support the ECB in its active involvement in college activities. The most recent college meetings that the ECB has attended have already shown that productive cooperation is going to continue on the same note. In generalterms,what do yousee as the mainchallengesfacing Europeanbankingsupervision? I think that it is important to ensure that the ECB is a supervisor that provides both high standards of supervision and a fair treatment of the supervised banks. There should be no doubts about the strictness and integrity of supervision, but a simplistic approach of "one size fits all" should be avoided at the same time. Decisions should be clear and understandable. The supervised banks should be given a proper say and a high level of cooperation should be ensured. As one of the youngestleaders in your country,you have already achieveda lot in your career. What motivatesyouandwheredo youdrawyourown inspiration? Many young people joined institutions and companies when Lithuania regained its independence and fought to build up an institutional framework and business environment of Western standards. As a child under Soviet occupation, I dreamt about the day when my country would become free and able to strive to standards of democracy and prosperity that we knew were given on the other side of the iron curtain. I am lucky that it came to be true, and that I've been able to play a part in this phenomenal transition. The enormous change that we have accomplished so far is the major motivating factor for me and my peers. International relations 3/3

Title: Interview to the daily newspaper Kauno diena
text: Interview of Rasa Platukien, Head of the Trade Division of the Investment Management Department of the Bank of Lithuania, to the daily newspaper Kauno diena Rasa Platukiene, Head of the Trade Division of the Investment Management Department of the Bank of Lithuania, is interviewed by Ruta Grigolyt. Interview published on 16 April 2015 in the daily newspaper "Kauno diena"  Why has the amount of Lithuanian gold reserves not changed for many years?  Gold constitutes a small part of the financial assets of the Bank of Lithuania (Bank of Lithuania). 5.8 t of gold was accumulated in interwar Lithuania, which was recovered in 1993 after the restoration of Lithuania's independence. The size of the gold reserves has never been changed by the LB and does not intend to do so. On the one hand, when comparing the long-term yield of alternative investments, gold is a financial asset with relatively low incomes and with large price fluctuations, so investing a large part of the portfolio in it would be risky. On the other hand, in the presence of global economic or political cataclysms, gold is better protected from the risk of losing purchasing power than any other currency. Therefore, while maintaining a stable amount of gold, LB ensures a fairly good breakdown of the total financial risk and effective management of financial assets.  What is the value of gold reserves in euros today?  At the end of the first quarter of this year, the market value of LB's gold reserves was about EUR 206.4 million. Euro. The market value of gold reserves changes daily, since it depends on constant changes in the price of gold, reflecting the dynamics of economic, political, technical and other aspects of the market. For example, ten years ago, the price of a gold Troy ounce fluctuated around 500 euros, in the autumn of 2011, at the height of the global financial crisis, troy ounce reached already 1.9 thousand euros. dollars,and today this price fluctuates around 1.2 thousand. Dollars. (Investment gold of 99.99 hallmarks is measured in Troy ounces (31,103 g).  Is there any thought of increasing gold reserves in the future?  On 1 January 2015, the Bank of Lithuania joined the fourth Agreement on Gold between the Central Banks, which obliges the participants in the above-mentioned agreement to coordinate the change in the amount of gold reserves they hold for five years and not to significantly reduce the gold reserves they hold. After five years, this agreement is usually reviewed and renewed. The central banks of all euro area and some other European countries are attached to this agreement.  When adopting the euro, Lithuania had to transfer a seemingly 1.3 tonnes of gold to the European Central Bank (ECB). How is this done if the available gold reserves have not changed?  With the introduction of the euro in Lithuania, the Bank of Lithuania became a member of the Eurosystem (consisting of the ECB and the national central banks of the EU Member States that adopted the euro currency) and transferred its contribution to the Eurosystem's foreign reserve assets: 85% in US dollars and 15% in gold. The share of the gold transfer amounted to about 1.6 Tonnes. It should be borne in mind that the part of the reserves transferred by the Bank of Lithuania to the Eurosystem continues to be the property of the Bank of Lithuania and, consequently, of the State, just that this part of the assets is managed together with the Eurosystem. In order to maintain a stable amount of gold reserves managed by the Bank of Lithuania itself, the transferred amount of gold was purchased on the market.  Why is part of the state's foreign reserves generally considered gold, from what point of view and in what cases is it useful?  Gold is like a kind of stabilizer that helps to break down the risks, that is, not to store all the eggs in one wicker. As mentioned earlier, in the event of economic or political cataclysms, the prices of most financial investments fall, while gold, on the contrary, represents the status of "safe investment" and therefore becomes more expensive. However, in calmer times, the value of gold can fluctuate greatly.  How is gold reserves earned? "There are two ways to earn. The first is by placing gold deposits with central banks and earning interest. The second way is more complicated - gold for a fixed period is exchanged for another currency (for example, US dollars or euros), and for that period, a security is purchased for the funds received, which gives a higher return than the gold deposit. When the deadline comes, the financial flows are returned to the initial stage. Before investing gold, as in the case of all financial assets, the Bank of Lithuania signs international agreements with counterparties and manages the counterparty and other related risks at various limits.  To whom is the income from gold reserves allocated when it was previously allocated to ensure the stability of the litas?  As provided for in Article 23 of the Law on the Bank of Lithuania, 70% of the three-year average profit of the Bank of Lithuania shall be transferred to the budget of the Republic of Lithuania. Most of LB's income consists of income from the investment of financial assets, and therefore also from the investment of gold. In total, LB has already transferred EUR 475 million to the state budget. and most of this amount has been transferred over the last six years. The main purpose of the financial assets of the Bank of Lithuania before the introduction of the euro was to ensure the stability of the litas exchange rate by maintaining the coverage of litas issued into circulation. Currently, financial assets are intended to cover the euro turnover in Lithuania and to ensure the stability of the financial system of Lithuania and the euro area. As you know, the Bank of Lithuania is one of the 19 national central banks in Europe, emitting the euro and participating in the development of the monetary policy of the euro area. Gold reserves make up a small part of the financial assets of the Bank of Lithuania.  What makes London's storage facilities so reliable and useful? Is there any part of the stock elsewhere as well? Why couldn't they be kept in Lithuania?  All LB gold is stored in London, in the vaults of the Bank of England. Historically, it has been formed that the main financial centers for investing (and storing) gold in Europe are Paris and London. On the one hand, national gold reserves are traditionally protected in a country whose geopolitical position, size, military power and other circumstances can ensure the security of gold. On the other hand, gold reserves are stored where it can be easily invested, without incurring additional costs in the physical transportation of the invested gold when transferring ownership from one hand to another. When the gold storage location of most market participants coincides, the invested (loaned or temporarily sold with the obligation to buy back later) the precious metal physically moves from one pile to another in the same storage facility, in the case of the Republic of Lithuania  at the Central Bank of England, London. Why? Let's remember the story. 19221940 The part of Lithuania's gold reserves stored in the central banks of France and England did not change its owner even during the Soviet period de jure and was de facto returned to Lithuania after the restoration of the independence of the Republic of Lithuania. It is easy to infer what would have happened to these stocks if they had been stored in Lithuania. Secondly, bringing the gold home is inevitably associated with the additional costs of securing protection and transporting it. In addition, gold investment opportunities and potential earnings would be lost in Lithuania. It should be noted that since 1999, more than EUR 38.5 million has been earned for gold investments. Euro.  What information about gold reserves is classified for security reasons?  International ethical standards do not allow to reveal the details of a particular transaction. All other information is public, published in the Annual Report of the Bank of Lithuania, in the annual financial statements, as well as in the report submitted twice a year to the Seimas of the Republic of Lithuania. Relevant statistical information on changes in the financial assets of the Bank of Lithuania, including gold reserves, as well as the Financial Asset Management Policy (185 KB download icon) are published on the Website of the Bank of Lithuania.

Title: Speech at the opening of the conference Macroprudential Policy: The Role and Experience with Credit Flow Restrictions
text: 03/08/22, 14:41 Speech by Vitas Vasiliauskas, Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania at the opening of the conference "Macroprudential P.. . ffl'I:) LI.ETUVQS B,AN KAS SpeechbyVitasVasiliauskasC, hairmanof the Board of the Bankof Lithuaniaat the openingof the conference"MacroprudentiaPl olicy:The Roleand Experiencewith CreditFlowRestrictions" 2015-07-03 Goodmorning,dear Colleagues, Welcome to Vilnius, everyone. And thank you for your interest in our event. Please, believe me - and this is not just a polite phrase to begin a speech with - that we (my colleagues and I) truly highly value this opportunity to meet you all - speakers, panellists and participants with macroprudential policy expertise - everyone who kindly accepted our invitation to share their vision and experience. And of course, thank you to our keynote speaker Vftor Constancio, Vice-President of the European Central Bank, for joining us. According to the programme, we will have an a, of 1 intensive day today. I guess and I hope that we will hear different and, perhaps, even conflicting views. Nevertheless, despite differences in views, the fact that we have all gathered here and now means "we are all in this together". And I believe that we share more than just an interest in the same subject of systemic risks. In my view, an additional "common factor" is our shared understanding of responsibility. Let me justify my presumption : economists - both classics and modern stars - often argue that one of the most dangerous conditions for every economy at any time is a bad attack of economic pessimism. This opinion is voiced each time economic growth and credit expansion slow down. 03/08/22, 14:41 Speechby VitasVasiliauskas,Chairmanof the Boardof the Bankof Lithuaniaat the openingof the conference"MacroprudentiaPl ... I do not dare argue with classics such as Keynes, but is an attack of economic optimism a less dangerous state? History has shown that over-optimism distracts attention from spotting risks on time. Therefore, when growth curves skyrocket, the silent consensus is: this time is different. Ladies and gentleman, It is not worth counting how many such "different times" we have already had. However, it is really worth noting the similarities among all of these "different times". First, there were no institutions with an explicit mandate to monitor and prevent systemic risks in the financial sector. Second, although no one was at fault, the final payer was always there - society and the tax payers, including those who had no relationship either with financial institutions, or credit. Recently we have lived through an unprecedented series of bank failures that have cost too much. Far too much. Some societies suffered losses related to bank crises that amounted to nearly half of their GDP. Dear colleagues, I do not intend to dedicate my speech to a review of the recent crisis. I would rather point to one more consistent pattern, common to all regions and all times. From ancient times, people and states attempted to regulate credit markets, more so than the businesses of bakers or shoemakers. They tried, in modern words, to ensure responsible lending and borrowing. Remember the old rules and Shakespeare's moneylender - the one who required a "pound of flesh" as collateral? You certainly know the regulatory actions of the US government after the Great Depression, as well as the past efforts of European countries. But why then does history repeat itself? One of the possible answers is that because we tend to forget lessons from the past. If I had to illustrate the developments of the financial sector and its regulation in a chart, it would be a wavy curve. Crisis, followed by stabilisation followed by tightening of regulation. Then - recovery and increasing voices about "overly" strict regulation that hinder credit growth, plus, persuasion that the sector is capable of regulating itself ...This would be followed by "loosening of the bolts". Possibly even exaggerated deregulation . 03/08/22, 14:41 Speechby VitasVasiliauskas,Chairmanof the Boardof the Bankof Lithuaniaat the openingof the conference"MacroprudentiaPl ... on one side and maintaining - on the other side - the implicit or explicit government guarantees for the financial sector and consumers. This would naturally lead to irresponsibly aggressive expansion and recurrence of the "boom and bust"... This is how it repeatedly happened in the past. And that should mean that soon we will face headwinds against regulation. Does this mean that history will repeat itself? There is no answer yet. We are creating the answer now ourselves. However, one thing is clear: our situation is unique in several aspects. First of all - responsibility. Yes, I have already mentioned this word. And I will mention it again, since, in my understanding, it is the key word and the core element of macro-prudential policy. We know well that although the term "macro-prudential" was mentioned in the late 1970s, in many countries it has been recognised that no single authority had the responsibility, powers and instruments to monitor the financial system as a whole and respond to systemic risks. There were analyses and theoretical discussions, but only a few examples of practical action. Now, the responsibility is assigned. To us: central banks, supervisory agencies, financial stability committees. In many cases the institutions that are represented here today sought this responsibility and assumed this duty voluntarily. This reflects our attitude and gives hope to believe that this time could be different indeed. Another thing that supports this expectation and distinguishes the current situation is our mandate. Together with the duty, we also obtained real powers to move from theory to practice. Lithuania was one of the first countries that started using a set of private credit flow restrictions. In 2011, the Bank of Lithuania adopted responsible lending standards, which put limits on the loan-to-value and debtservice-to-income ratios as well as loan maturities. If you are interested, my colleagues will gladly share their insights about the impact of these instruments. Most likely they will say: if these tools had been in place before the burst of the 2008 real estate bubble, the credit cycle would have been much smoother and the negative consequences would have not been so dramatic for our economy. The last decade's boom in housing prices in Lithuania went together with the sharp rise in the credit supply and was certainly accelerated by this short-sighted generosity. . 03/08/22, 14:41 Speechby VitasVasiliauskas,Chairmanof the Boardof the Bankof Lithuaniaat the openingof the conference"MacroprudentiaPl ... To illustrate: from 2004 until 2008, private credit was growing much faster than the Lithuanian economy and the credit-to-GDP ratio doubled from less than 40 per cent to almost 83 per cent! During the same 4-year period the real housing prices increased by 240 per cent. It was the sharpest increase in the Nordic-Baltic region that ended with one of the deepest falls: the real prices dropped by 1/3 in a bit more than a year and a half, ravaging not only the sectors involved, but also the economy as a whole. People say: every cloud has a silver lining. It was a drama and at the same time - a lesson. We took the lesson seriously. We took actions. It surely was not, is not and will not be simple. The former chairman of the United States Federal Reserve Bank, William Mcchesney Martin, once famously said that his job was to "take away the punch bowl just when the party gets going". He talked then about "leaning against the wind" of inflation, but his famous quote has been recently used to illustrate the main objective of macro-prudential policy. People do not like change in general. Especially if it restricts them. We experienced that in 2011, when we started to apply our responsible lending standards for the first time. We also faced it recently, just after we announced our intentions to modify these standards. However, we are determined not to lose direction. Especially now, when the prevailing environment of particularly low interest rates requires special vigilance. We have to be prepared for interest rates returning to the "normal" level and help both lenders and borrowers always estimate their loan repayment capacity in a prudent way. As it has been said, our strategy should be "tilting against the wind" of building-up imbalances in the credit market. Dear Colleagues, In the beginning I raised the question: pessimism or optimism? I do not know the answer as to which attacks are worse. However, I know what is better - a prudent balance, caution and responsibility. I wish us all of this in our daily work. And I wish you an interesting day and fruitful discussions. And now I will gladly pass the microphone to our honourable keynote speaker. . 03/08/22, 14:41 Speechby VitasVasiliauskas,Chairmanof the Boardof the Bankof Lithuaniaat the openingof the conference"MacroprudentiaPl ... Vftor Constancio is the Vice-President of the European Central Bank, with more than a decade experience as Governor of the Banco de Portugal. He is a policy maker and academician, one of the key people in European banking who kindly agreed to share his views with the participants of the first conference on macro- prudential policy organised by Lietuvos bankas. Please, Vftor, the floor is yours. Financial stabilitY..

Title: Speech at European Economics and Financial Centre
text: 03/08/22, 14:38 ffl'I:) LI.ETUVQS B,AN KAS VitasVasiliauskas.Speech at EuropeanEconomicsand FinancialCentre I Bankof Lithuania VitasVasiliauskasS. peechat EuropeanEconomics and FinancialCentre 2015-09-28 Goodafternoon,dear LadiesandGentlemen, It is my great pleasure to be here with you today. Thank you for your invitation. And thank you for suggesting a topic that shows your interest in my country . As far as I know after consulting your website, I am the second Lithuanian to speak at the European Economics and Financial Centre. The first one was the former Prime Minister of Lithuania, Mr Brazauskas, who in 2002 presented here Lithuania's intentions to join the EU. Today, after a little more than 10 years, I am representing the same but, in a way, completely m,of 1 different country - a member of the EU, NATO,euro area. A country on its way to joining the OECD. Our dynamism makes it hard to know where we will be when the third Lithuanian speaks here. But I am keen to share some thoughts on where we are today and where we are going to be in the foreseeable future. I am also going to offer you an update on developments in the Baltic region. Lithuania's entry into the euro area has completed the entry of the Baltic region as a whole. Therefore, today there is a new sense in seeing the three countries - Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia - as a single economic area. And, finally, whether we are in the euro area or not, we all live in a globally interconnected world and depend on each other's successes and failures . So I suggest that we also spend some time discussing the future of the Economic and Monetary Union and the financial sector developments in the global context. 1/10 03/08/22, 14:38 VitasVasiliauskas.Speechat EuropeanEconomicsand FinancialCentre I Bankof Lithuania Our latest big economic event is the euro. "Why? And why now?" - I was asked these questions many times. I believe they might be particularly natural here, in London, and now, when the euro area is facing, let's call it, some specific challenges. Let me explain our reasoning. First, in contrast to the UK,we were obligated to adopt the euro under the Treaty. Even more important was our long-term objective to ensure monetary policy consistency. Before the euro adoption, we had a currency board arrangement for more than 20 years. For more than a decade our currency - the litas - was pegged to the euro. And for more than a decade we participated in the Exchange Rate Mechanism II, which is like a "green room" before entering the euro area. These two unilateral commitments had become an anchor of financial stability and discipline. They have also proven our adherence to rules and showed that it is possible to successfully function under the fixed exchange arrangement even during the most difficult periods. The hard peg to the euro meant that Lithuania de facto was in the euro area. The next deJurestep allowed us to eliminate the speculative exchange rate risk component in our borrowing costs which - especially in difficult times - imposes a harmful burden on both the state and the private sector. Before the final decision, the Bank of Lithuania carried out a quantitative assessment of the possible impact of euro adoption. Our experts also assessed how much we would have saved if we had adopted the euro in 2007. The findings were quite impressive: in total, the government and private non-financial sector could have saved up to 0.8 per cent of GDP in 2007-2012. Additional economic rationale: more than 2/3 of our goods export goes to the EU. About 40% of it - to the euro area; 80 per cent of FDI inflows to the Baltics originate in the EU countries and about 45 per cent of it in the euro countries. We expect that in the longer run, the introduction of the euro will have a positive impact on our foreign trade. The experience of other countries shows that the euro introduction increased their trade by 5 to 10 per cent. We also expect that the common currency will be conducive to cross-border capital investment, even though empirical evidence is surrounded by more uncertainty in this area. 2/10 03/08/22, 14:38 VitasVasiliauskas.Speechat EuropeanEconomicsand FinancialCentre I Bankof Lithuania Of course, this does not complete the list of our motives. I will be frank: we did have some other motivation as well. If you are interested, I will be glad to discuss it with you later. Now I would like to turn to our economic characteristics and I dare to say: the Baltic countries are an example of countries that are perfectly accommodated to work within a single currency area. Why do I say that? First - the flexibility of markets, especially the labour market. We have surprised many counterparts, including international institutions, rating agencies and investors, by the high degree of responsiveness of our labour markets. Before 2008, wages in the Baltic countries were growing at a particularly high rate. Wage growth was clearly outpacing productivity. However, when the crisis struck, the labour market changed its course. The wage-productivity gap closed very swiftly, in slightly more than a year. Most of the adjustment took the form of cuts in nominal wages. In Lithuania, for example, wages were reduced by 10 per cent in just two years. It is also remarkable that these sizable wage cuts took place in both the private and the public sector. Such a prompt adjustment helped us maintain competitiveness. And it clearly proved a high degree of flexibility, which is so necessary for countries operating within the single currency area. Another key prerequisite for sustainable development, especially in the absence of monetary sovereignty, is prudent fiscal policy. It is true that fiscal governance in the Baltic States did not always follow the highest standards. During the pre-crisis boom, very strong domestic-demand-led growth created a fiscal illusion that cyclical revenues could be turned into permanent current expenditures. The deep downturn that followed showed how wrong this assumption was. However, every cloud has a silver lining. The economic crisis-related turmoil also gave us a lesson and we learned it. We undertook unprecedented fiscal consolidation that amounted to around 15 per cent of GDP The consolidation was largely expenditure-based. It included cuts in public sector wages and social benefits (pensions, maternity, unemployment and illness benefits). On the revenue side, the standard VAT rate and excise duties were raised, a number of VAT exemptions were abolished. 3/10 03/08/22, 14:38 VitasVasiliauskas.Speechat EuropeanEconomicsand FinancialCentre I Bankof Lithuania This was painful, but effective. The consolidation helped us restore market confidence and regain access to capital markets. All in all, we have managed to maintain our fiscal houses in order. The Baltic fiscal deficits and debt levels are well below the EU "benchmarks" of 3 and 60 per cent. Looking ahead, it is clear that our fiscal policy will be affected and, hopefully, improved by the recently reformed, largely rules-based fiscal governance framework that has been agreed upon at the EU/euro area level. I am confident it is a step in the right direction. But it is crucial and our/Baltic experience supports this view - to have the political and institutional capacity to "own the rules and adhere to them. The challenge is to ensure that this capacity is always in place, both in difficult and good times. In this regard, I believe we need to exploit the full potential of the existing framework first, before embarking on a more radical reform of the fiscal system as a whole. I will come back to this later. Dear Colleagues, You probably remember: when the turmoil in 2008 started, economists were busy debating what shape this crisis was to assume? Some said it had to be L-shaped - which meant a long-lasting recession. Some predicted a quite optimistic U scenario. Others warned against W. And all agreed that the most desirable would be V. Regretfully, not many countries were able to recover in that V manner. The Salties were among those that did. We were back to growth already in 2010. Even in 2012-2013 - when the euro area was having a second recession - the Salties managed to sustain relatively strong growth momentum. Recession in Lithuania lasted only 5 quarters. Since 2009 each of the Baltic countries grew by 20 per cent. How did we do that? A flexible labour market, prudent fiscal policy and high competitiveness - these are our characteristics that definitely served the economy best and gave a strong foundation for future developments. Up until now the Salties are demonstrating strong resilience to external headwinds. Following somewhat weaker growth in 2015, all three Baltic countries are expected to reach approximately 3 per cent annual growth in 2016. Ladies and gentlemen, 4/10 03/08/22, 14:38 VitasVasiliauskas.Speechat EuropeanEconomicsand FinancialCentre I Bankof Lithuania That was a brief flashback at our - I dare to say - true success story. Now let's turn to what is seen in the horizon, having to admit that the world around us poses a number of challenges. By saying "us" I mean all of us - the Baltics, the Euro area and the EUas a whole. In 2016 economic growth in the Baltics is expected to pick up due to gradually improving outlook in our major trading partners - countries of euro area and other EUcountries. Economic growth in these countries is expected to benefit from favourable financing conditions, low commodity prices and improving prospects in other developed economies [namely, US], resulting in greater domestic demand and demand for our exports. The latest macroeconomic outlook was presented by ECBonly a few days ago. The good news is that despite challenging environment the euro area is showing moderate signs of improvement. GDP growth is positive in a number of core economies - Germany, Italy, Spain. Short-term economic activity indicators, like PMI (purchasing managers index), retail sales, show signs of returning confidence. A number of factors are supporting the positive outlook. Low oil prices and substantial monetary policy easing are among the most important ones. But this is not a reason to relax. Estimations for all external regions have worsened. The first region to mention is emerging Asia. Huge over-lending, that lasted for years, and the current rebalancing, that takes place in China, makes increasingly uncertain whether China's growth will stay in line with the projections. Another notable factor is that Russia's economy is expected to shrink by around 4 per cent. Given low commodity prices, the economic growth in Russia and surrounding CIS economies will take time to reemerge. The US economy is also growing at a significantly slower rate than it was expected. The projections have been revised by around one percentage point. No doubts these developments will influence Europe. 5/10 03/08/22, 14:38 VitasVasiliauskas.Speechat EuropeanEconomicsand FinancialCentre I Bankof Lithuania What can and needs and is being done to answer these supressing impacts and to enhance the positive ones? Every policy-making institution has its objectives, responsibilities and a set of policy instruments at its disposal. As a member of the Governing Council I would like to start with the ECB. First of all I will remind you of 2014 - a year when growth in the euro area was sluggish, inflation was at risk of becoming persistently low and the ECB,in response, started to substantially intensify its monetary policy easing. Remember June 2014. The ECBfurther cut its policy rates and announced Targeted Long-Term Refinancing operations, designed to restore lending to the real economy. In September 2014, the ECB once again lowered its main refinancing rate to 0.05 per cent and announced two additional programs - the Asset-Backed-Securities Purchase and Covered Bonds Purchase Program both aimed at further credit-support. Finally, in January 2015 the ECB announced that it would start implementing an Extended Asset Purchase Program (or Quantitative Easing) later in March. Of course, it is still too early for doing final sums. The ultimate measure of success will have to be based on the assessment of inflation adjustment towards our medium term target. Clearly, more time and evidence are needed for such insights. But I feel quite comfortable stating that some positive results are already apparent. Firstly, in addition to sovereign yields, bank lending rates have decreased, including, and more substantially so, in certain periphery countries. Secondly, after years of decline, credit to the private sector has finally started to grow. In line with that, and for the first time since 2009, survey evidence shows that the number of SMEs reporting improvement in their access to credit is higher than the number reporting the opposite. All of these indications suggest that our policy has contributed to a general improvement in financial conditions. Eventually, these positive developments should help us achieve the main policy objective. It is likely that accommodative ECB policy supported confidence in the private sector. 6/10 03/08/22, 14:38 VitasVasiliauskas.Speechat EuropeanEconomicsand FinancialCentre I Bankof Lithuania According to surveys conducted by the European Commission, the economic sentiment indicator in the euro area has already increased in 2015 and reached its highest level since 2011. In some periphery countries such as Italy or Spain the economic sentiment indicator has approached or even exceeded its pre-crisis levels. Other optimistic news - after 3 years of contraction, credit growth in the euro area has resumed. Historically low interest rates substantially reduced the loan repayment burden. This factor, along with rising confidence increased the private sector's demand for credit. At the same time, better economic sentiments and better economic prospects have urged banks to soften their lending standards. According to the ECB's surveys, since 2014, more banks have already been softening rather than tightening their lending standards. In this environment in 2015 the growth of credit in the euro area has returned to positive territory. In July the growth of credit was already 4.5 percentage points higher than a year ago. And what is more, the trend of growth is expected to be maintained. Even in member states in which deleveraging is still ongoing, credit contraction is slowing down rather quickly. Sustainable credit growth is a crucial ingredient to this growth. Therefore, recent trends in the credit market, indeed, fuel some optimism. At the same time, the latest events in global financial markets have significantly raised uncertainty and heightened the risk of market contagion. Just a month ago, we witnessed a strong worldwide sell off in equities that started with a crash in the Chinese stock market. The event was preceded by a relatively minor devaluation of the yuan and somewhat weaker economic data, but that was sufficient to hike investors' concerns. And the financial contagion was very swift in a single day major global financial markets suffered declines unseen since the recent financial crisis. Worries over China have exerted downward pressure on global commodity prices. Oil prices reached a 6 year low. That, in turn, has worsened the prospects of commodity exporters, typically emerging markets, depreciating their currencies and prompting capital outflows into safe havens. The resulting surge in volatility in the financial markets was the highest since 2011. It reminded us that markets have become very sensitive and ever more exposed to volatility. 7/10 03/08/22, 14:38 VitasVasiliauskas.Speechat EuropeanEconomicsand FinancialCentre I Bankof Lithuania By delivering very low interest rates and elevating financial asset prices, very accommodative monetary policy may have contributed to this sensitivity. That complicates the policy environment as higher volatility may feed into lower market confidence and lead to sudden corrections in asset prices. Hence, we should be mindful of the recent events and the challenges that may lie ahead, especially in the context of potentially diverging monetary policy directions by major central banks and worsening growth prospects in some emerging market economies. In the context of increased market volatility, we should be more than ever mindful of systemic risks. In the Euro Area, they are mainly rooting from low growth and the prolonged period of low interest rates. First - reversal of risk premia. Over the last years, the premia of holding riskier assets decreased substantially. An abrupt increase of the premia to their historically normal levels could result in significant losses for holders of relatively risky assets. That is especially relevant in the environment of rather low market liquidity. Second - weak profitability. With interest rates at historically low levels, financial institutions [such as banks or insurance companies] are facing prospects of weak profitability. While the low interest rate environment persists, the pressure to "search for yield" and accumulate more risks is building up. And finally - debt sustainability. The prospect of weak economic growth in the Euro area would pose debt sustainability concerns for countries where the debt-to-GDP levels are extremely high. As was already mentioned, the ECB's monetary and credit easing is helping to restore confidence and growth in the more vulnerable and highly indebted countries, such as Spain, Portugal or Italy. This is certainly a good news, but not a happy ending yet for this story. Even if we have found some shortterm solutions that appear to be effective, it is important to admit: we still badly need long-term decisions and I would like to particularly underline action. In dealing with the recent economic challenges the EU has proved its abilities to think strategically and take on ambitious commitments. But, at this stage, the most important thing is the ability to stick to what was agreed. Just to illustrate: at the moment only 5 EU member states (the UK and Lithuania are not among them) fully comply with the provisions of the Stability and Growth Pact. Another sad example: last year none of the EU states fully addressed any out of 157 country-specific recommendations. And that is despite all the assessments [presented by the Commission] showing, that EU GDP could be raised by 6 per cent after 10 years, if the EU member states reduced by half the observed 8/10 03/08/22, 14:38 VitasVasiliauskas.Speechat EuropeanEconomicsand FinancialCentre I Bankof Lithuania "structural gaps" vis-a-vis the best performers in a number of areas. Why is the EU track record in complying with the agreed rules so poor? And, most importantly: how to change that? The so-called "5 Presidents Report", published in June, aims at preparing the next steps towards completing the Economic and Monetary Union. We have to acknowledge: the Report has already fuelled a hot debate that is more important today than ever before. At the same time, it reminds us that every suggestion, even if it comes from the EU presidents, requires both open-mindedness and critical thinking. I have in mind, first of all, the proposals to create new institutions: a European fiscal board and national competitiveness authorities. In my understanding, the main problem today lies not in the lack of institutions, but in the complexity of the rules, which makes compliance weak and monitoring difficult. My take-away point is: we should spend less time on creating new procedures and institutional bodies. What we really need is strong political will to enforce what we jointly agree on by strengthening and making more binding the existing rules. I would like to turn now to the core idea of the EU- the single market. Too often we tend to forget that the potential benefits of the single market are still not fully reaped. The capital market is a proper example in this case. The degree of its development widely varies across the EU,although all, even the best performers, could gain from deeper financial integration. First, there is no need to mention to this audience that well-developed capital markets reallocate capital more cost-efficiently across industries and countries. Second, in Europe we are used to seeing banks as the main source of capital. However, they are often reluctant to take the risk of financing innovative projects, especially by start-up companies with high potential, but no credit history. The development of integrated EU-wide private equity, venture capital, and equity markets is essential to secure financing that might benefit long-term growth. And finally, well-functioning capital markets could distribute risks more efficiently. This role is extremely important in the absence of fiscal redistribution capacity in the EU. 9/10 03/08/22, 14:38 VitasVasiliauskas.Speechat EuropeanEconomicsand FinancialCentre I Bankof Lithuania At the moment, the EU Capital Markets Union initiative lacks content, but we are looking forward to seeing the Commission's concrete proposals on this priority promised by the end of the month. A related initiative aimed at strengthening the single market in financial services is the banking union. And it proved our abilities to offer a systemic response. While a typical legislative process in the EU lasts 1.5 years, the agreement on the Single Supervisory Mechanism was reached within 6 months and it became operational last autumn. The second pillar of the new EU banking policy framework - the Single Resolution Mechanism - is expected to become fully operational next January. However, the quick start faces the risk of a slowdown. The Single Resolution Fund has no credible backstop so far. The Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive is still not transposed into national law in a number of member states. Moreover, we still lack the third pillar a truly European Deposit Insurance Scheme. It is noteworthy that the idea of integrating national deposit guarantee systems was suggested by one of the UK's institutions back in 2009. In response to the Icelandic banking crisis, the UK's former financial supervisor - the Financial Services Authority - urged to consider introducing pan-European arrangements for the deposit insurance of banks operating across-border in branch. I strongly believe this was a good and timely idea. I am also convinced that without the third pillar the banking union will be incomplete and that we do not really need another lesson to show us that a "halffinished" project may fail to deliver. Therefore, I am really happy to share with you the feeling that the European Commission has recently renewed its policy efforts and that there is a real possibility to have a fully-fledged banking union in the near future. The Commission has promised to present a legislative proposal on the common deposit guarantee system before the end of this year. 10/10

text: 03/08/22, 14:55 ffl'l:) READ.ETUVQS B, HELMET Interview of Vitas Vasiliauskas, Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, to the daily newspaper Lietuvos zinios, 291/04/2016 Bank of Lithuania Interview of Vitas Vasiliauskas, Chairman of the Lithuanian Bank's Management, to the daily newspaper "Lietuvoszinios", 29/04/2016 2016-05-04 Vitas Vasiliauskas, Chairman of the Lithuanian Bank's Management, is interviewed by DaliusSimnas. The interview was published in the daily newspaper "Verslozinios" on 29 April 2016 and on the portalVZ.LT2016 on 2 May 2016. What was it like in 2015 for banks and other credits Bodies? 2015 was profitable for banks. Profit compared to In 2014, it grew by about 1%. Return on assets for several years now remains about 8-9% . However, I would point out that the profit indicator was achieved last year by cutting costs, there was a particular decline in administrative, and in some in banks - the cost of IT maintenance . Obviously the traditional interest income of banks has decreased. This should come as no surprise, because in all segments m,of 1 interest decreased, and commission income also decreased. This is an objective factor. Adopting the euro in Lithuania the number of currency exchange operations decreased, the fees for international transfers decreased. And these are the new challenges that banks have to deal with adapting to the new circumstances in the medium term. On the other hand, the consistent growth of the loan portfolio is pleasing . At the beginning of 2015, there was no impetus in the credit market, but in the second half of the year there was a turning point. Now the loan portfolio is growing at a rate of 4-5%. Crediting is more active for households and businesses. So I would say that the trend of loan growth is quite sustainable and positive. Unlike banks, the insurance sector suffered a loss last year. Why? The insurance market itself grew by 7.4% last year (to 645 min . Eur of written contributions), the growth rate was more or less in line with the bank of Lithuania's forecasts. But the year was indeed unprofitable for insurers. Experienced a total of 13.4 minutes . euro loss . Life insurance received 10.1 minutes. Eur profit, but non-life insurance had a loss of EUR 23.5 min. 1/6 03/08/22, 14:55 LietuvosbankovaldybospirmininkoVitoVasiliauskointerviudienrasiui Lietuvoszinios",2016 04 291 Lietuvosbankas In the field of non-life insurance, there remains a tendency for premiums to grow, but the activity is not profitable. After entering the market competition has increased for new entrants. It's good for consumers, but it's not a question of the stability of life market participants. We are watching the market re-share and hope that new entrants will change the trajectory of unprofitable activity in this segment. The Bank of Lithuania has expressed concern that the recovery of the investment life insurance is too low and that the benefits that the customer receives are only linked to the tax advantage. Is it true that the Bank of Lithuania proposes to waive the residential income tax (GPM) exemption for this type of insurance? Market participants, for their part, pointed out that the efficiency of life insurance in Lithuania is only 0.5% and is 8 times lower than the EU average. The GPM exemption in terms of unit-linked life insurance works quite effectively compared to the returns provided for this product. We argue that the main benefits that a holder of an investment life insurance policy receives are more related not to natural returns, but to the application of the benefit. And here we see the problem. So that's what our suggestion is all about. We do not believe that the state is rich enough to contribute in this way to the penetration of life insurance, which, despite the relief, is already expanding very little. It is my deep conviction that investing is one thing and insurance is another. When you mix two things, their combination can be quite interesting. Even before I came to work at the Bank of Lithuania, I had investment life insurance. I had to terminate the contract prematurely, so my experience wasn't good. It was a very good lesson, and so far I try not to mix two different products. If I invest, I invest. That's how I'm trying to build up something for the future. And if I want to protect myself from certain risks, then I take out insurance. What are some of the biggest challenges the banks are facing today? The biggest dilemma for credit institutions today is the low-interest environment. It poses certain challenges to the stability and returns of the financial system in the medium term. Of course, this is a challenge for banks to adapt to new business conditions. I really do not think that in the near future we can expect a transformation in an interest environment, that low interest rates will suddenly start to rise. Analysis of macroeconomic indicators shows that the low-interest environment will remain in the period of the next few years. We observe the fact that even central banksinvest funds in riskier assets to obtain higher returns. 03/08/22, 14:55 LietuvosbankovaldybospirmininkoVitoVasiliauskointerviudienrasiui Lietuvoszinios",2016 04 291 Lietuvosbankas Yes, it is true, given that the return on government securities (WP) is now greatly reduced, and shorter-term WP also generates negative returns, which affects the performance of central banks. We we are no exception and are looking for where to earn, but I would emphasize that the main central bank the task is to have fairly liquid funds so that they can be used if necessary. First of all, we raise the goal of keeping investments stable and liquid, and then we are already thinking about return and profitability. What changes to the regulation of the credit market are foreseen in 2016? I would draw attention to the financial services provided, where several new aspects have emerged. We have presented a package of additions to the Law on Payments regarding the legal regulation of the main account. We aim to install a basket of services at a fixed price. We also envisage transposing the provisions of the Housing Loans Directive into national law. This is about the obligation for lenders to provide more information to mortgage borrowers. A clearer distinction will be made between the concepts of fixed and non-fixed interest rates. A prohibition is provided from borrowers to require them to have an account in the lender's institution or to accumulate funds in a pension fund. Of course, mention should be made of the reform of credit unions. A package of laws on such a reform has reached the Sejm, as well as an alternative bill has been submitted. The proposed reform is supported by the majority of credit unions, i.e. more than 60 credit unions operating under the umbrellas of the Central Credit Union of Lithuania. So, here we really have a common understanding. The consolidation of this sector, centrally provided services, the strengthening of the capital of credit unions and centralized financing of activities could significantly change the quality of credit union services and in the long run a fairly strong, albeit niche, service provider among credit institutions could appear in Lithuania. This year, we also plan to submit for consideration the Draft Law on Crowdfunding, as well as to introduce measures to promote the capital market. Bank customers complain that this year there has been an increase in transfer times in some banks, although it has been declared that since 2016, after switching to SEPA's system of euro settlements, they will not experience any inconvenience.A memorable case when st. Over the Easter weekend, the money could not be credited to the bank account even for fourparas - from Friday to Tuesday. Why do bank customers encounter such atroversy? We've done our part to the end. We've cut rates and campaigned for the three largest banks to stay in the SEPA-compliant retail payment system we administer. Our system, compared to the system used by the big banks (european banking association), is certainly more advanced, better, faster. This is a system of almost instantaneous crediting of money. In my opinion, blaming everything on SEPAis completely wrong. All the more so because the main banks had the opportunity to choose. They made a business decision based on the cost. By joining payment systems, of which their primary banks are shareholders, they received an economic effect, but consumers suffered. It's obvious. 03/08/22, 14:55 LietuvosbankovaldybospirmininkoVitoVasiliauskointerviudienrasiui Lietuvoszinios",2016 04 291 Lietuvosbankas Small banks, credit unions have stayed with our system. They can certainly offer a lot better ones, I think conditions, and I hope that the big banks will pay attention to this. We are always waiting for them to return and offer the best pricing options. It is always more convenient for the user to fly on a direct flight than with a transfer. In the case of the three big banks, consumers now have to fly with a transfer. It's really uncomfortable for the passenger, in this in the case of a bank client. You say the decisions are made. Is it realistic for large banks to change their minds? If the customer is a value, the business should be flexible. I think a good opportunity to rethink our strategies will be through discussions with us about the national payment strategy. We plan to bring its draft to the market this year, and we will talk with market participants about the provisions of the document. We are hearing some signals about the Scandinavian banks, namely Nordeos' possible withdrawal. r The Baltic states can be of interest to otherstrategic investors? Of course, the emergence of new entrants in the market would be welcome. We receive such timid glance signals. Whether we receive new systemic entrants from outside Scandinavia will depend on the further economic environment in the region and on the economic situation and geopolitical environment in the euro area as a whole. The signals we are receiving today do not give me reason to say that we will have new large banks. It would be more realistic to assume that we will have new niche market participants, for example, consumer credit institutions, alternative financing entities, various funds. I would point out that the financing of a business on the capital market through the issuance of securities may increase. Also, if large foreign investors come to Lithuania implementing certain infrastructure projects, it is possible that banks will follow them. Kokiusinfrastrukturos projektusturiteomenyje? I am talking about the port of Klaipeda, Klaipeda Free Economic Zone and investments there. Do you have a community of Chinese investors? Yes, I am talking about Chinese investors. As a rule, Chinese business moves with Chinese banks. I'm talking about crediting corporate clients here. I would doubt that what's new will come into the retail banking segment. 03/08/22, 14:55 LietuvosbankovaldybospirmininkoVitoVasiliauskointerviudienrasiui Lietuvoszinios",2016 04 291 Lietuvosbankas It seems that the appetite of companies to borrow seems to be growing, but the possibilities of obtaining a loan at the bank for a small business are still Limited. Why? After the crisis, the banks, as we know, have changed their lending policy and are currently quite cautious about the credit possibilities of companies. The whole point of the monetary policy of the European Central Bank (ECB) is to push the banking sector towards the crediting of small and medium-sized enterprises. The ECB's quantitative promotion programme has been in place for more than a year. In March, it was extended until March 2017, and the scope of the programme was extended with a view to the purchase of value paper from EUR 60 billion. up to 80 billion Eur per month. If the program continues to expand, can we say thatit works? It is clear that the quantitative easing programme works primarily through falling interest rates on loans, as well as falling borrowing costs for governments. And all this stimulates economic growth. Since the start of the ECB's quantitative easing programme (March 2016), the positive impact on euro area gross domestic product has been 0.5 prae. item, the amount of interest on loans fell by 0.6 prae. Point. Those trends are positive, but it is clear that each stage of the expansion of the programme has less and less of an impact, but this does not mean that there is no need to move forward in the light of the economic environment as a whole. Surveys of economists show that the EC may take additional stimulus action in the last half-year. Is he right? As far as the extra steps are concerned, I think it is early to speak. I am inclined to first assess how the decision of the ECB's Governing Council in March this year works. Only a corresponding juxtaposition of that impact of the programme with the evolving economic situation could decisions be taken on the continuation of monetary policy. So my position would be to monitor the implementation of the measures adopted and, if necessary, to react. What are the new quantitative promotion measures available here? There is a lot of discussion about the so-called helicopter money. Does the ECB sometimes plan to inject money directly into the eurozone economy? This idea can be discussed in economic forums, but I think it is still a long way from practical implementation. In my opinion, the issue here is not primarily for the central banks, but for the governments, because I understand this as a fiscal policy instrument. What do you predict for the Eurocursus? Willit remain favourable to the exporters of Lithuania and the euro-economies as a whole? First of all, it should be talked about the fact that the exchange rate of the euro, its relationship with other currencies and, above all, with the US dollar is not any goal of monetary policy. 03/08/22, 14:55 LietuvosbankovaldybospirmininkoVitoVasiliauskointerviudienrasiui Lietuvoszinios",2016 04 291 Lietuvosbankas At least in the short term, any changes could hardly be expected, but the exchange rate of the euro, without there is no doubt that it also depends on the most important decisions of the central banks, in particular the decisions, which are accepted by the ECB and the US Federal Reserve System. The current fuel for the euro, in my opinion, does indeed contribute to increasing the competitiveness of the euro area, and for us as an exporting country, this is important. The totality of low oil prices, the euro exchange rate, and moderate economic growth in Lithuania's main trading partners, I believe, also contribute to the growth of our economy. The exception is Russia, but our business has already swallowed that bitter pill, and if the situation there were to improve, our export positions would only get stronger from this, but in fact we have already reoriented our export markets. If the ECB were to continue to expand its quantitative promotion programme, would it be logical to assume that such steps would weaken the euro's exchange rate against the other currencies? So.
