Verslozinios",2017 12 151 Lietuvosbankas Interview of Vitas Vasiliauskas, Chairman of the Lithuanian Bank Administration, to the daily "Verslozinios", 15/12/2017 2017-12 -15 Vitas Vasiliauskas, Chairman of the Lithuanian Bank's Management, is interviewed by VyttautasV. Zeimantas. The interview was published on December 15, 2017, by the portaleVZ.LT of the daily newspaper nVerslozinios. What are the international and local trends in the economy, in the financial sector, this year, and what are the most important issues In the next year? In the international sphere, we can state that economic growth in the euro area has gained momentum and its outlook is stable. The euro area economy has grown a , of, eighteen consecutive quarters and these trends will pass on to the market. Inflation rates are still a long way from The objective pursued by the EuropeanCentre Bank is an inflation rate close to, but not exceeding, 2%. But with the real there are no economics. Lithuania is distinguished from the euro area countries by higher inflation. As we predicted,average annual inflation this year is 3.4%. Both the increase in excise duties and the minimum wage contributed to its growth. Next year, we are entering a period of preparation for the new EUfinancial perspective. The volume and composition of preparations that nourish the financial circulation may change, so Lithuania may also have to adapt to new ones Circumstances. From the point of view of the political cycle, the next year is also important enough - opportunities should not be missed to finally adopt and implement structural reforms, about which there is a lot of talk. Looking at the demographic prospects of ten years, I see possible tectonic fractures. We need to prepare properly so that later we do not grieve that we have not done something. That would be the wish for next year. Are you talking about what kind of tectonic fractures are you talking about? 1/5 03/08/22, 14:53 LietuvosbankovaldybospirmininkoVito Vasiliauskointerviudienrasiui Verslozinios",2017 12 151 Lietuvosbankas About demographic processes that are difficult to influence. To date, in our country, there were more young people who complement the working-age group of the population than the older population leaving it. This year, for the first time since The number of supplements and leaves of the restoration of independence is about the same, and in subsequent years complementary there will be fewer and fewer than those who leave. In other words, labor is beginning to retreat. It's a strong demographic break. The next breakthrough awaits already in the near future - in about ten years. This is a fairly rapid increase in the number of pensioners per working person. To date, that number has been able to be maintained more or less stable due to the increase in the retirement age and the increasing participation of the population in the labour market. However, in a decade's time, this figure is likely to start to increase, even if we continue to raise the retirement age. Thus, we will have another factor that has an unfavourable effect on the labour market, in addition to the relatively high net emigration and the mortality rate of the working-age population. The three main things that can help combat these negative trends are taxes, the pension system and education. They affect competitiveness, the social environment. The Bank of Lithuania has taken an initiative that is not unusual for central banks, which is to talk about tax reform. Why are you taking this theme? We have set ourselves the goal of being a centre of excellence, and public finance is one of the areas where we can recruit our expertise. We have put forward our proposals for pension reform, we are talking about taxes, but it is not us who will make the decisions. We do not want to take someone's place under the sun, but for a small economy like Lithuania, it would be very important to have a consensus on the three areas mentioned above. How do you propose to change the tax system? The level of redistribution in Lithuania is low, there is not enough money to finance certain public services at the proper level - to pay pensions, we see tensions in the education sector and in society in general. Our proposals are focused on how to increase redistribution. First of all, the potential of VAT is underutilized - the shadow in Lithuania, according to various estimates, is 16-25%, which is big money. The taxation of labour in Lithuania is clearly too high. If we look at social security contributions as a tax, and otherwise it does not go out of our way to look at it, because contributions are taxed without any restrictions and there is a 'ceiling' for benefits, then the taxation of workers is very progressive. One of our cardinal proposals is to combine the contributions of the employer and the employee "Sodra" and make them an employee's contribution, while at the same time increasing the gross salary. These are emotional, motivational things, but they can change a lot. Nor are we exploiting the potential of direct taxes - we have too much variety of tax regimes - over 50 personal income tax breaks. The possibilities of taxes on cars, real estate are also not exhausted. We have been hearing recommendations from the European Commission on these taxes for several years now, https :// ristatai/lietuvos-ban ko-boards-firsti ninko-vito-vasi liausko-interview-d ienraseiui-verslo-zi nios-2017-12-1 5 2/ 5 03/08/22, 14:53 LietuvosbankovaldybospirmininkoVito Vasiliauskointerviudienrasiui Verslozinios",2017 12 151 Lietuvosbankas We can expect an international monetary fund, a similar recipe, from the OECD. These are classic taxes, and I don't see the reasons why they should not be in Lithuania. Eloquent example - according to budget revenues from assets and income of taxes, which last year amounted to 5.7% of GDP, Lithuania was second to the end of the EU. Without an increase in redistribution, nothing will happen, because other problems associated with it - social exclusion, income Inequality. Without solving them, we cannot move forward. Why should the affluent population contribute to greater redistribution? After all,they have earned everything themselves? We see what is happening in society - it votes with its feet. If we are talking about the part of society that lives from capital, then it should be concerned about how much demand we can expect in Lithuania. If there is a drastic reduction in the number of bread-eaters in this corner of the earth, it will not be possible to employ capital and earn returns either. I am not talking about social unrest and influence on geopolitical matters, changes in the relationship of society with its state. If you ask me if I am prepared to pay higher taxes, I would answer yes, because I am convinced that the more a person earns, the proportionally more he has to give away. Not to the government, not to some faceless organization, but to their own community. After all, all of us are a state. You need to share with those who are less fortunate in life at the moment, who are weaker. Otherwise, we will go to nowhere. And how do you propose to change the pension system? The issues of the pension system and taxes are interlinked, they need to be dealt with together - individually they do not "fly". The Bank of Lithuania has put forward proposals on how to solve the problems of sustainability and adequacy of the pension system, the most important of which would be: the introduction of personal accounts, the introduction of more flexible forms of work and retirement of the older population, and the promotion of adequate levels of accumulation. Personal accounts in "Sodra" in real time would indicate how much a person has accumulated for old age. This measure would help to strengthen the link between contributions paid by a person during his or her lifetime, and benefits received, increase the motivation to pay contributions. More flexible forms of balancing the work and retirement of the older population would be a response to the demographic situation. As the population ages, a longer stay on the labour market would help to address labour shortages and poverty among older people. . lb.lt/lt/kaibos-interviu-p regulations/lietuvos-ban ko-board-first ninko-vito-vasiliaus ko-interview-d ienraseis-verslo-zi nios-2017-12-1 5 3/ 5 03/08/22, 14:53 LietuvosbankovaldybospirmininkoVito Vasiliauskointerviudienrasiui Verslozinios",2017 12 151 Lietuvosbankas Looking at demographic trends, the standard of living of future pensioners compared to what they had when working, does not turn pale. If trends do not change, around 2060 the ratio of the average salary to the average pension will fall from the current almost 50% to about 30%. Here it is only about the first tier. If an adequate level of accumulation is not ensured, the second tier will not sufficiently compensate for the losses. I would especially like to to stress that the reform of the pension system must not be opposed to the first and second pillars of pensions. Important and annuity issue - now paid annuities look very poor. Betjeigu nesukaupei,negalitiktis didelioanuiteto? Yes, the level of accumulation is especially important. Accumulating only 2% of the amount of income tax, we can not count on a decent annuity at the end of the accumulation period. Real returns are determined not only by accumulation. This concerns both the administration fees and the assumptions and figures that are used to calculate the annuity. The size of the annuity is also related to the issues of the methodology for calculating it, but in any case, we would see room for greater efficiency in this area. Due to demographic problems, will Lithuania's economy be stuck with 0% growth? I don't think we're going to face zero growth, it's just that growth will be much slower. If it is not possible to turn the demographic problems in the right direction, then it remains to increase productivity. It needs to be increased regardless of demographic trends. And other unavoidable structural things related to productivity are science, education, the tax system, public safety and, in general, the level of happiness in the country. Can LB reduce inflation in Lithuania? Monetary policy is common to the euro area, so euro area figures are important. Inflation varies from country to country in the euro area, as is the case in the US states. However, decisions are taken jointly with the whole region. In addition to monetary policy, there is a macroprudential policy that affects credit, and through it - inflation. Macroprudential policy is implemented through two instruments. Some are directed to the capital of banks, various reserves, others - to the demand for credit. The latter can also be attributed to the Responsible Lending Regulations. Lithuania at the top of the economiccycle. Are there any plans to require banks to increase their countercyclical Capital? We "measure the temperature" every quarter, later this month we will announce what we think. But in general terms, in good times it would be useful to think about a certain reserve so that in bad times it can be abandoned. What questions are currently lying on the European CentralBankostal? . lb.lt/lt/kaibos-interviu-p regulations/lietuvos-ban ko-board-first ninko-vito-vasiliaus ko-interview-d ienraseis-verslo-zi nios-2017-12-1 5 4/ 5 03/08/22, 14:53 LietuvosbankovaldybospirmininkoVito Vasiliauskointerviudienrasiui Verslozinios",2017 12 151 Lietuvosbankas Personally, I believe that the euro area will reach its growth potential next year. The ECB has so far decided to to extend the asset acquisition program, but since January, bond acquisitions have been declining from 60 billion to 60 billion in 2018. Eur per month to 30 billion. Eur per month. I believe that the horizon of the end of the economic stimulus programme - others year. The Basel Committee, together with representatives of the largest central banks, agreed on basel 11-1 new requirements for the capital of the bank. Risk assessment models and many other things are changing. It is very welcome that the changes in all countries start at the same time - from 2022 - and are being implemented within five years. Everything was just being created, new laws were being passed, learning was the most from his mistakes . That period is very different from the present day . Where do I see the similarities? I would single out three areas. The first is the lack of regulation or regulatory flaws . Credit unions are specific financial institutions . They are cooperative . They need specific management . The public understands credit unions as small banks. Yes, they carry out the same activities as banks, but they are managed on completely different principles. Without realizing this, I think certain mistakes have been made, and there have been loopholes in the regulatory law. This allowed credit unions not to operate in accordance with all the principles of cooperative activity. The second similarity. At that time, bankers Qie were either young or old-generation professors) only learned private banking: how business is done, how clients are worked with, how risks are managed. There was a stage of learning . Credit unions basically operate in the regions. And for people there, too, a lot of what else is new, complex . But the business of a credit union is like a bank, they take deposits, they lend. All those principles of risk assessment, capital liquidity, operational management are mandatory for the credit union. That's what they needed and needed to learn and know. The third point is malign activity . From those times we can recall some banks that collected deposits and did not return. And in the current failed credit unions there were cases of malicious activity. 1/5 03/08/22, 14:53 EkonomikosirfinansiniostabilumotarnybosdirektoriausG. ?imkausinterviuDiena.Itl Lietuvosbankas - What are the differences between bank and credit failure? - A credit union is a cooperative financial institution. The specifics of the coop are different from the bank. The main one is difference in management. In a credit union, one member - one vote. Each member of a credit union is an owner with one vote. How to ensure an effective, common democratic solution? Here is the point, task for modern society. - There is no shortage of advertising in the public domain that credit institutions can have higher interest rates than in banks... - In principle, yes. The difference is that when you come to a credit union, you must become a member of it, you must buy shares. But let's remember the case of ''Taupkas?', when offering "Deposit Plus" with the purchase of additional shares, the credit union did not disclose to depositors all the risks of the product. When a credit union is in trouble, let's call it, they just lose that share. As a shareholder, it would lose shares in any other company if it went bankrupt. The credit union lives on financial intermediation: it accepts deposits, lends and invests. Depositors are part of that business, but they must understand that by bringing their money together they become the owners of that company. Not only the owners, but also those responsible for its activities. They are obliged to participate in the activities of the credit union. The question is how depositors perceive this. There is a great lack of perception. One of the tasks of credit union reform was to change the law that at least 5 prae must attend the re-meeting. seamen. It's a small number, but it didn't participate that much either. Therefore, it used to be that in a cooperative society decisions were made by an absolute minority of more active seamen, who could turn the activities of the union in one direction or another. And this is wrong and intolerable, because a credit union is democratically governed by all seamen. Second. The credit union system began to be developed in 1995, when there were difficulties with banks. After the crisis of 2008, it grew at a very fast pace, and the activity was unprofitable every year. If the activities of any company are unprofitable, this indicates that something is wrong with the business model, the sustainability of activities. The seamen, who are the owners of credit unions, kept adding new deposits and shares to them and seemingly ensuring their further activities. However, such activities are not sustainable in the longer term. Another thing. In large cities, the activities of some credit unions have degenerated. They would imitate pseudo-banks with inadequate risk management or even investment companies. It so happened that some unions had invested most of their assets in securities. When the very essence of a credit union is to serve its customers, take deposits from them and give them loans, and not be an investment fund. Another evil: what was called the capital of credit unions was actually like the form of a deposit. You could buy shares, make a deposit, and withdraw both the deposit and the shares again. In financial activities, there will always be certain fixed costs. After all, it costs risk management, accounting, investment risk management, customer service, etc. A picture with a credit union on every campus may look nice, but that activity was unprofitable. It was clear that cooperation between these credit institutions was necessary. This has happened and is happening in other countries. And we had a system where you could belong to one Central Credit Union or act separately. One of the important changes was the strengthening of cooperation between cooperatives, i.e. between the unions themselves. It was clearly stated in law: if you want, well, turn into a bank, nothing bothers you. Five credit unions have chosen that path. But if you want to be a cooperative body, then act as a cooperative, have normal capital, participate in the mutual guarantee system, the stability fund, join the Central Credit Union, and if you want to - follow your partner. If you have another business vision, work together, share common ideas. This is what happened: previously there was one central credit union, after the reform another central credit union appeared. - It was hoped that this area of finance would be stabilised once the credit reform was completed. However, every year the Bank of Lithuania restricts and even suspends the activities of road users. Last year was a record year, with five unions announced the collapse of five unions. How did that happen? - The course of reform needs to be remembered. In mid-2016, laws regulating the activities of credit unions were passed. At the end of 2016 and the beginning of 2017, the assessment of the asset quality of all unions and the analysis of the results took place. Time was given for credit unions to correct operational deficiencies. The implementation of the reform began with a white sheet - if credit unions merge into a common system, you need to know who your friend, partner is, what is his real financial situation. The time was given to correct the situation, to attract capital. By the way, there was a huge distrust of each other among credit unions. Yes, last year there were many supervisory actions of the Bank of Lithuania. After the assessment of the quality of the property, it became clear who was who. After evaluating everything, it became clear which credit unions are insolvent, they did not manage to continue their activities. With the launch of two central credit unions this year, the situation is completely different. I believe that this reform has greatly changed the perception of the participants in this market, the managers of credit unions. We see a huge optimization of activities, an increase in efficiency. For example, last year, after a long period of time, credit unions worked profitably. I will say more - last year's profit exceeded the system's previous total profits combined since their inception in 20 years. This shows how unpaved the soils of efficiency were in this system and how it needed good regulation. For credit unions to be what they have and hopefully want to be. - This means that the managers of the credits stopped buying Bentley and otherprabangiuscars, urien?ra Necessary? - Bentley occurs when there is a lack of internal control and owner responsibility. The natural question is who needs the cooperative company Bentley, what benefits it brings when all the customers are also seamen, i.e. the owners. It can be said that let's leave it to everyone's conscience. However, the beginning of everything in a cooperative company is the involvement of seamen in the activities. In the absence of this, unfortunately, cooperatives can have problems. There are also good examples in Lithuania. We also have strengthened provisions of the law. But the worst thing is that the seaman only has a deposit and interest on it, he does not understand that he also acquires a financial instrument along with the share and becomes the owner of a credit union. It's not that I want to or I don't want to, it is - I have to be involved in governance. It is necessary that both depositors and borrowers take an interest in the management of the union, demand dissemination, where meetings are held, go and participate in them. Because that's where the decisions are made about their money. If people don't attend meetings, 20 more active seamen can turn the direction of the credit union 180 degrees. It doesn't matter that there are 1Ot?kst in it. Here, as is the vote of the people when the president of the country is elected. When a person comes to vote, he has one vote. If you didn't come, you didn't vote, then your voice is empty. So does the union. I would associate low activity with the Soviet era. The fact is that we have a low degree of community. In the apartment building, we no longer recognize our neighbors. And in the states with cooperative traditions - Holland, Austria, Germany, especially in their smaller towns, there are communities, there are community banks. Maybe it is not necessary to be present for everyone, but perhaps the father of one is present, the representative of the family is present. Communication in credit unions is completely different. And with us, everyone is scattered. - it seems to people from the sidelines that some of the credits, as in the commercialbanks of 1991-1995, contained some of the swindlers, for whom it was only important to collect deposits from the people and to take advantage of the money. Especially in smaller cities... - Before the reform of credit unions, there were more than one such case. One of the directions of the reform was the merger into central credit unions. And that was one of those heavy parts. Because self-control is needed. Then not only seamen are interested in their union, but also partners - unions - in each other. How does business management, loan risk management, what is the financial situation, who are the managers, etc. This ensures that cases such as Bentley purchases are intolerable. Another thing, there was a central credit union before, but a little maybe toothless. After the reform, central credit unions received more rights and powers to take measures to prevent risk factors in credit unions if necessary. text: 03/08/22, 14:53 rt, U.S. 11::)BANK Lietuvosbankovaldybospirmininko??angin? kalbaper Ekonomikoskonferencij? l Lietuvosbankas Lithuanian Bank Management President's advanced speech at the Economic Conference 2018-09-17 Lithuanian pension system: how to ensure socially justifiable and sustainable pensions? Vitas Vasiliauskas, Chairman of the Lithuanian Bank's Management Dear colleagues, like-minded people and potential opponents, lt3 l 111111n111111111l!i1l1l1\l AND KONOMIKO Welcome to the second Economic Conference of the Bank of Lithuania and watching us online. a , of, Goodmorning, dear guests. Thank you for joining us at the second Lithuanianeconomy conferenceof the Bankof Lithuania. We are delightedto haveyou here. In deciding to hold these annual conferences, we have set an ambitious goal: we want and strive not only for original insights and interesting discussions (although - I will not hide - we also hope for this), but also for a tangible result. There are also analyses and evaluations of proven experiences in real life. All of this is summarising and summarising the number of conclusions and proposals that would help to address the most pressing economic policy dilemmas and to choose the best solutions. It is this goal that dictates the themes of our events as well. That's why we devoted our first conference last year to the issue of income inequality. We have consulted, analysed, and many have agreed that inequalities in income and, at the same time, opportunities grow from the roots that will be rooted in our tax and pension systems. We have agreed that they need to be reformed - immediately and in principle. Therefore, our topic today - the Lithuanian Pension System - is a consistent and logical continuation of last year's discussion. At the same time , this is also a newly soundedaccountuality. 1/6 03/08/22, 14:53 Speech by the Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania during the Economic Conference l Lietuvosbankas In a new way, because the ice has finally moved. The government undertook a reform of the pension system, which sooner or later, one way or another will affect everything and everyone - the daily lives of people, the public figures of the country finances and macroeconomic stability of the state. Therefore, this question undoubtedly deserved an exclusive attention from state institutions, the public and the media. The experts were also actively involved in the expert discussions and in the future, the Bank of Lithuania will participate, which understands its institutional obligation in this way. In short, our summary would be this: a step has been taken in the right direction. However - only a step. The work is far from finished, because, firstly, it is important not only to design solutions, but also to design them qualitatively Implement. Secondly, it is already obvious that even if we implement what has been started in a completely flawless way, the elements that we will have to improve remain in the Lithuanian pension system. I am thinking, in particular, of the need to increase the transparency of the Josiah tier, to strengthen people's confidence in it. In the future, these issues will become increasingly important. They will inevitably have to be dealt with, and - better sooner than later or... than ever. Therefore, already today we have to look a little farther beyond the horizon visible to the naked eye. And that is why, already in today's debate, I propose that we look at the perspective of our pension system not only on a scale of several years, but also on a scale of several decades. But before that - the starting position: the status quo of the Lithuanian pension system and the planned changes - Lithuania's the bank's assessment and some key proposals that we believe would help us to take the next steps in the direction outlined by the transformation. Colleagues There are two fundamental problems that we face. These are poor benefits now and the prospect of even poorer pensions in the future. About the present. The average old-age pension is close to the poverty line. The average replacement rate for residents receiving a Sodra pension alone - that is, the ratio between past labor income and pension - is only about 35 percent. ESvidurki - close to 50 percent. Approximately one in four of our seniors is at risk of poverty - according to the European Commission, according to this indicator, we are once again in the top three of the weakest countries in the EU. In such a third from the end - we find ourselves in a frequent position and even get used to it. But there is another important indicator - the ratio of pension costs per senior to GDP per capita. According to this indicator, we are, unfortunately, even lower. 2/6 03/08/22, 14:53 Speech by the Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania during the Economic Conference l Lietuvosbankas About the future. According to the calculation of the International Monetary Fund, without reforming the system, for self-study of old age the average replacement rate for non-accumulating residents would fall further in the coming decades - to barely 20%. This means that if we do not implement the changes, in a couple of decades of retirement, counting them in the current in terms of the value of money, it would be still about a quarter lower than today's. Poor old-age benefits today are due to several reasons. One of them is the low level of redistribution through the state budget. Last year, the amount of tax revenue collected in the budget in Lithuania did not reach 30 percent of GDP, while the EU average - almost 40 percent. By comparison, if we had collected at least as much tax revenue in 2017 as the EU average, the revenue to the budget would have been around EUR 2 billion. euros higher. A lot or a little? Almost as much as we spent on pensions that year in total. The level of redistribution (and at the same time budget options) is primarily a question of the correctness and effectiveness of tax policy. However, even if we implement the most effective tax changes, they alone will not be enough in the longer term, because in addition to redistribution, we have another disadvantage, and that is the extremely difficult demographic situation. Its consequence - the deteriorating ratio of the working population to the population of retirement age - means a heavier burden on public finances. In such circumstances, it becomes extremely important to create conditions and incentives so that the working and income-bearing population is aware of the situation and begins to accumulate a personal financial reserve for old age. Unfortunately, so far, to our knowledge, about 800 thousand people, and this is more than half of the total working population, accumulate only minimally or not at all for retirement. I wouldn't want to sound too dramatic, but... unlike a ticking time bomb, I can't call it that. Soon, our esteemed speakers will present the bigger picture - the practices of other countries and regions. We will probably see that our challenges are not unique: most developed economies have encountered or are still facing similar problems in one way or another. And although all of them have their own national peculiarities, and therefore everyone is looking for the most suitable solutions specifically for her, but in my opinion there are several common features that are characteristic of all the best-rated models. This is primarily an orientation towards long-term sustainability. Secondly, transparency and the resulting high level of trust of the population. These traits help to achieve the fundamental goal of ensuring the most even consumption, i.e. the level of income, throughout the entire life cycle of a person. The pension systems of our close neighbours - the Nordic countries - are mentioned among the best-rated in the whole world and have all these qualities. I am therefore pleased that we will soon have the opportunity to listen to Prof. Edward Palmer's report on Sweden's experience in reforming the pension system and moving towards a model based on personal accounts. Colleagues 3/6 03/08/22, 14:53 Speech by the Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania during the Economic Conference l Lietuvosbankas Analyzing the good practices of foreign countries, we note that in addition to the signs of similarity that I have already mentioned, they have one more thing in common: none of the pension systems that the population believes and trusts today has been created in one fell swoop. On the contrary, it was a long and daunting process, often carried out in stages and requiring consistency and focus. The Lithuanian pension system has also been on the road to larger or smaller reviews and reforms for some time now. And, although the meaning, and especially consistency and completeness, of some of the "reconstructions" could be argued, it is my belief that the latter decisions could create the preconditions for favorable change. First of all, the system is gaining more integrity. With the change in the structure of contributions to pension funds of the 11th step (by abandoning the part of the state social security contributions transferred to them), there are no reasons or pretexts for the artificial confrontation between pillars l and II. The second necessity is the likelihood that more residents will become involved in pillar II pension funds. This would mean an increase in the number of people who will be better prepared for the loss of their working income in the future. At the state level, this would contribute to increasing the sustainability of the pension system and help alleviate the demographic shock that inevitably lurks in the future. Thirdly, the important element for us is safer and more efficient hoarding. According to the data of the Bank of Lithuania, currently almost two-thirds of persons who participate in the 11th cycle accumulate in funds of risk that are not suitable for their age. Such a mismatch is a fundamental obstacle to the effective use of all the opportunities offered by the financial markets and to the accumulation of the maximum possible buffer for the future by assuming the most optimal level of risk. Therefore, the decision to introduce what is known as the principle of life-cycle pension funds in Lithuania is certainly welcome. By following it, we would implement the practice of "one size for all" (which, in fact, does not suit anyone), and the risk of investing accumulated assets would be applied to a certain stage of the accumulator's life, i.e. to his specific age. And finally, the cost of maintaining the system. The centralisation of the administration of annuities in Sodra - i.e. a non-profit institution - would make them cheaper. On the other hand, limiting the maximum allowable deductions of private pension funds would help the population to accumulate a higher income for old age. Will the planned changes be enough to ensure the long-term sustainability of the Lithuanian pension system and better adapt it to the needs of the population? Definitely yes. And definitely not. If we implement the ideas as intended, the model we are reforming can certainly become both more attractive and more reliable than the current system. However, if we are to align ourselves with the international frontrunners, we will not be able to get stuck on what has been designed so far. 4/6 03/08/22, 14:53 Speech by the Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania during the Economic Conference l Lietuvosbankas Having said this, I hasten to assure you: we do understand that stability is perhaps the greatest value of the pension system. However, according to our assessment, the Lithuanian pension system will need 3 additional improvements. The first should ensure a closer and necessarily more obvious dependence on contributions and benefits. This is an essential condition both for achieving the fairness of the pension system and for strengthening the incentives of the population to pay contributions. The second objective is more transparency. By strengthening the link between contributions and benefits, the 1st pillar of pensions should move towards a model based on personal accounts- the same as the one currently in place in Sweden, Norway, Poland and other European countries. The system organized in this way, ideally operating in real-time mode, would clearly depict the connection of a person's insurance premiums with the level of the future pension. A virtual personal account would, as a matter of fact, convince that unaccounted income is reducing the accumulated pension in the l-pillar and would encourage the payment of contributions. The third direction is informing and educating people. It is precisely the understanding of the system of accumulation for old age that is one of the surest ways to manage the risks of short-sighted choices. And such a danger, let us face it, may arise if, when the changes to the pension system come into force, people are tempted by a slightly higher income today, and not into the future. These three aspects that I have identified should be seen as pieces of the pension system puzzle, which are necessary and which are still lacking. Colleagues I do not want to become a "black" prophet, but the threats and risks faced by the Lithuanian pension system are really real. If we do not do the necessary work, we will face them - if not behind the nearest turn, then a couple more bends of the road. Therefore, in order to create a truly sustainable, I would like to stress - a sustainable long-term pension system that the people of Lithuania believe and trust, we must strive for consensus, consistency and determination for further steps. Today we have the opportunity and opportunity to talk about them boldly, openly and benevolently. I wish you rich discussions, valuable insights and conclusions that we may contribute to future decisions and Action. Thank you. 5/6 03/08/22, 14:53 Speech by the Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania during the Economic Conference l Lietuvosbankas Economic Analysis and Qrognose, Available. Title: Speech at the 20th anniversary event of the Managers' Club
text: Speech by V. Vasiliauskas at the 20th anniversary event of the Managers' Club Vitas Vasiliauskas, Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, participated in the Executive Club's 20th anniversary event "The Present That Creates the Future", where he spoke on financial and economic future issues. Dear Members of the Club, first of all , a sincere thank you for the invitation to participate in this businesslike festive event. I do consider the opportunity to join your society as an honour. Not because you're famous people, influential leaders, but because you're leaders  leaders who think about the future and build it. In saying this, I am thinking, above all, of the business success stories that you have created, without which a country's economic success story would not be possible. In fact, it is also difficult to imagine the future, which I am obliged to discuss by the topic formulated by the conference organizers. I'll admit, as a conservative central banker, I see the topic as the riskiest in the entire program. It's probably not worth explaining why. In these dynamic times, talking about tomorrow is a tricky affair. Predicting the year is a responsible job. Economic forecasts for a decade or even more so for a decade are a complex and often unreliable affair. A little challenge, a little adventurousness. But  man is man. And predictions are undoubtedly one of the forms in which the human desire to predict  to predict, to emerge, or to scientifically "deduct"  and to potentially control the future is manifested. It seems that the desire is innate: sources say that back in the times of ancient Egypt, people measured the boundaries of the nile patting and, based on these data, predicted the future harvest of grain. From today's perspective, these were nothing more than GDP forecasts. Understandably, we will not compare the methods and instruments of modern macroeconomic forecasting with the observations of the Nile. They have been matured and improved for many decades. But despite the progress, the economist community agrees  and consensus among economists is indeed rare  that making forecasts for a decade is extremely difficult, and even further predictions are simply unreliable. As a result, international financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund are also publishing detailed forecasts for a maximum of 5 years ahead. In an effort to maintain credibility  however, this is an essential 'resource' available to central banks  I will also focus today's speech on the forecast, i.e. the medium term. But before that is a picture of today's world, because, as the event's headline correctly proclaims, the future is created by the present. The global economy in 2017 was in its best condition in a decade. We are also growing rapidly this year. We can see that, despite unrest and uncertainty, growth in the medium term should remain stable. However, due to the emergence of new trade restrictions, world trade volumes at face value will be somewhat slower in the near term. In addition, differences in the pace of development are beginning to appear in the world between the regions. What does this prophesy? I will not be surprised to say that the global balance of power is changing. Moreover, it is possible that the outlines of a new, or more precisely, multipolar world order, which have not been seen for several centuries, are emerging. The 19th century was the time of the British Empire. The 20th is the apogee of U.S. influence. In the 21st century, U.S. dominance is challenged by Asia. The challenge is bold. But it's just as serious. As a result, it receives very diverse, even contradictory, but always very serious reactions. Let's remember: Pivot to Asia  "Turning to Asia". This was one of the main lines of politics of then-US President Barack Obama, which signaled two things. The first is the recognition that economies that seem to have grown on the yeast are very promising. The second is the U.S. determination to strengthen ties with them to counterbalance China's growing influence in the region. The current U.S. administration line and related environment are different... Dunda's trade war drums, new U.S. import tariffs come into effect, are already in place today for more than half of the imports of Chinese goods. If we add what is currently expressed as intentions or threats, then already in the near future tariffs can be applied to practically all goods entering the United States from China. China, although with less room for manoeuvre (since it exports almost 4 times more goods to the UNITED STATES than it imports from it), did not "owe" any debt - it imposed similar restrictions on the vast majority of imports from the United States. The European Union has managed to stay on the sidelines in this battle and even to sit down with the US representatives at the negotiating table. This is something that, even if the outcome of the negotiations is not yet clear  for example, if the US were to implement threats to 'burden' the EU's strategically important sectors such as the car industry with additional tariffs, the possibility of atmospheric warming would remain extremely real. To sum up the above: the reactions of the two US administrations are radically different. But what is common between them is that in both cases it was China that occupied a crucial place in U.S. foreign policy. And the reason in both cases is probably the same. It is at least partly determined by economic processes, and from them the forecast is derived that already this year China should overtake the eurozone in terms of economic size and find itself in second place, immediately after the United States. According to the estimates of part of the experts, the balance of major economic powers will continue to change. If their forecasts are confirmed, with the decline in the weight of European countries in the global economy, in 2032 it will be possible to achieve a significant increase in the number of european countries. India would break out in third place, while China would overtake the U.S. and establish itself in the first position. Europe's biggest economic power , Germany, would fall from the fourth position to the fifth position. It's true that, recalling what I've already said, I would put this insight in the category of debatable. First of all, the 32nd year remains farther away than the horizon of reliable forecasts aspires to. Secondly, China, like all of us, faces its own challenges and is looking for ways to counter them. At the same time, other countries, regions and communities are still looking for solutions to their issues. Therefore, today we cannot yet know what those decisions will be or (in some cases) who the decision-makers will be. For these reasons  i.e. for a million unknowns  I wouldn't dare bet who would overtake whom in what year. However, in view of the obvious, I would venture to argue that the bright mono-leadership that has been observed for several centuries should be replaced by a new  multipolar economic order. This means that we cannot ignore the rise of new centres of economic power. And we certainly shouldn't wait until either the 32nd or the 22nd, because even today  in 2018  we have enough information to think about the principles on which we will base our partnership with leaders in Asia. For us Europeans, this means, above all, the need to rediscover our place , that is, the European Union, in a new global order. If we assume - and it is certainly likely - that the power rivalry and tensions between the US and China will intensify in the future, the European Union could perform the extremely useful function of a support column here, preventing the bridge between the Far East and the West from breaking. After all, on the one hand, we have a transatlantic partnership, economic, financial and security ties for many decades with the US. On the other hand, we are discovering more and more common points in our relations with China. For example, the European Union is already cooperating with China today on the Reform Initiative of the World Trade Organisation. It was thanks to the Mediation of the European Union that China joined the Paris Climate Change Agreement and remained a part of it even when the UNITED STATES decided to withdraw from the agreement. There are more such examples of communion. The circumstances are indeed favourable: the European Union is in a unique position where it can play the role of a successful and influential mediator. What's in it for us and how do we achieve it? Colleagues in the context of tectonic shifts, we must soberly assess our place and power in the world. Ten years ago, a quarter of the world's population lived in Europe. Today, only one in ten people on earth is European, and this part is declining. Unfortunately, this circumstance does not give reason to expect that the economic, political and cultural influence of our land will spontaneously increase in the coming decades. Rather, the other way around. We must therefore find new ways of preserving a place at the negotiating table of the influential. And first of all  to make sure that the retaining column, perhaps capable of supporting the fractured U.S.-China bridge, does not crumble on its own. I am one of those who believe that it is deeper integration that is the response to negative tendencies: fragmentation and the rise of populism. In turn, an essential component of deeper integration is more effective economic governance. It is therefore encouraging, at least for me, that recently the debate on the need to strengthen the foundations of economic and monetary union has become both more active and intense. They are also likely to be fuelled by the impending end of the term of office, both by the European Parliament and by the Commission. However, even in this case, the fact that decisions on the reform of the European Stability Mechanism are expected as early as December is very good news. I will not torment myself with the details, I will just say that the essence of this reform is to enable countries, as soon as they notice the emerging risks of financial stability, to receive a package of preventive support  a kind of 'credit card'. It is not necessary to use the card funds  the mere fact of having it can calm investors' fears about the country's solvency. This means preventing a possible crisis and strengthening the financial stability not only of that country, but also of the euro area. Another very important detail: such a "credit card" would be available only to "progressive" members who follow the rules and manage their public finances in a disciplined manner. It seems that additional funding from the European Union's Single Resolution Fund should also be approved in December. This will make it clearer that public budgets, and that is to say, taxpayers' money, will not be needed to rescue failing banks. The prospect of a European deposit insurance scheme. If a breakthrough in this debate finally takes place, it would be a great achievement in strengthening the Economic and Monetary Union. European deposit insurance would equalise the protection of depositors throughout the Community the protection of every saver would be guaranteed for the banking sector throughout Europe. Such a mechanism would allow for the development of more efficient international banks that exploit economies of scale and would strengthen confidence in the stability of the Community's financial sector. It would also be a message that both the world and Europeans need that the Community is capable not only of generating ideas, but also of realising them, or, in other words, of completing what it has begun. In this particular case, it would be a banking union project. Finally, the euro area budget. On the table are various ideas and projects put forward by both the EU institutions and national governments. The ambition varies from 0.3% of GDP, which, when converted into euro, would amount to around 30 billion, to even 'a few' percent of GDP, which would amount to tens of billions. I do not think that today we have the opportunity to discuss these ideas in more detail. However, I cite them as proof that Europe, firstly, recognises the need for greater solidarity. Secondly, they are aware of the need for deeper integration. And thirdly, she has not lost her ambitions to preserve and possibly expand her international economic influence. For example, deeper economic integration and a wider distribution of risks between Member States would increase the use of the euro as a reserve currency. While the euro remains the world's second most important reserve currency, the gap with the US dollar remains huge. Moreover, the share of foreign exchange reserves in euro in the world fell from 24% in 2005 to 20% last year. In order to reduce the backlog behind the US dollar, which accounts for more than 60% of all foreign exchange reserves, we must strengthen the international role of the euro. Will it work out? I have just mentioned some positive signs. However  even against their backdrop  there is no sense that the prospects for deeper economic integration may drift away. The window of opportunity for more important transformations may narrow as early as May 2019. European elections. On the other hand, seeing that the Member States are not complying with today's commitments, it is difficult to hope that a significant breakthrough will be achieved in terms of risk-sharing and greater financial solidarity in the future. Here's the proof. The European Commission makes recommendations to Member States based on their own commonly agreed rules. We see a sad picture showing that the number of recommendations implemented is decreasing every year. In 2012, significant progress was recorded in the implementation of 11% of the recommendations. In 2016, out of 86 recommendations, only two progressed significantly. Last year, progress was made in implementing just one recommendation (out of 76). An even sadder example of recent weeks. I have already mentioned that decisive negotiations are under way on the most important reforms that can strengthen  or not  the Economic and Monetary Union. And at the same time, we are hearing a case of extremely gross disregard for the agreed fiscal rules. What is also special about this case is that the government, which envisages a significant increase in government spending, openly admits that it understands that its budget will violate the requirements of fiscal discipline. In other words, the agreement is broken deliberately. Such an open confrontational tone, which is unprecedented in the history of the Stability and Growth Pact, certainly does not strengthen the idea of economic integration. And without her, it would be difficult to successfully play in the "top league". Dear ors painting already looks complicated, I will risk complicating it even more. Because, along with the global shifts in power and european internal processes, there are other  no less interesting changes that might be more correct in this case to call transformations. We are talking about the future, so if we do not want to be caught unprepared for it, we cannot ignore them. Already in the next ten years, we will feel what the 4th Industrial Revolution brings, which is fundamentally reforming the structure of the economy and the principles of operation of its individual sectors. Naturally, this change does not bypass the financial sector either. The wave of fintech  or FinTech  is an illustrative example of this: artificial intelligence, blockchain, big data solutions are already changing the face of the financial sector. And it's clear that it's going to change even more fundamentally. In the first half of this year, global investment in FinTech companies amounted to almost 60 billion. US dollars. This means that in the first half of this year alone there were 1/3 more investments than in the whole of 2017 and 3/4 more than 5 years ago. From this I would conclude that investors see the prospect of innovation in the financial sector. And that investment in this area is already reaching a scale that has the potential to change the financial sector in the long run. We hope for the better. First of all, that innovative fintech solutions in the financial sector will stimulate competition. I will base this insight on the example of the Lithuanian payments market that is closest to us  the lithuanian payments market. With the merger of the two banks, the large trio have a share of the big trio in our payments market of about 80%. Our assessment is unequivocal: this concentration is wrong. However, the good thing is that new alternative  i.e. non-bank  payment service providers are entering the market. We are encouraging their arrival, and we already have about 115 Fintech companies in the LT financial market. The number of electronic money companies alone has increased more than 5 times in the last year and a half. Obviously, "the ice has moved." What is the result? The share of electronic payments provided by non-banks at the moment already exceeds a tenth, and trends show that this share is increasing with acceleration. And it's likely to increase, with about 40 more new applications for FinTech licenses currently being evaluated. In other words, FinTech is throwing a glove at traditional financial institutions. These, in order to preserve positions, will have to take into account new realities and the changing needs of the client. They will have to change their business models, ideologies and behaviours. In fact  it's already changing. For example, two banks, which until recently were extremely skeptical, are starting to provide an instant payment service. This means that the FinTech glove is raised. Another expectation that is associated with FinTech is the democratisation of the financial system. The World Bank estimates that 1.7 billion will be spent on the project. people (more than a fifth of the Earth's population) still do not have access to elementary financial services  say, they cannot open an account in a bank. FinTech solutions are what can change and change this situation fundamentally. This time, a further but particularly convincing example is sub-Saharan Africa. Almost half of the global mobile settlement market goes to this particular region. The number of mobile wallets actively used is 70 (seven and zero) times more than in Europe and Central Asia combined. Africa is a world leader in the field of mobile payments, and this is what made it possible to significantly increase the number of residents of the continent, who began to actively use financial services. Fintech has given Africa a unique opportunity to "jump through" the traditional banking phase and move from cash directly to electronic alternatives. I hope that these technologies will also change the relationship of other societies with cash, which costs those societies a lot. I also hope, or rather, that I have no doubt that Fintech tools can significantly expand the range of sources of credit. It is estimated that the global peer-to-peer lending rate, which is growing by about 50% annually, is expected to reach EUR 900 billion in 2024. US dollars. An impressive figure that can favorably affect both the availability and prices of credit, and the traditions of credit in a broad sense. Colleagues I'm guessing the benefits will be enough  you're definitely not the audience where you should talk about the opportunities offered by innovation. I have no doubt that you have also heard about the risks. However, I must remind you of them, because new financial products, new channels for their presentation, new IT solutions requiring data opening and digital connections to a bank account represent new challenges for both service providers and their recipients. How to overcome them? Not to stand up, but to open up to innovation. Tame and recruit for the benefit of oneself and the public. We at the Bank of Lithuania follow precisely this principle and, dare I be glad, it works. More specifically, a few years ago we set ourselves the goal that the Bank of Lithuania would work not only as a steward  which is inevitably part of our duty  but also as a partner in the financial sector. We advise and advise beginners. We recently installed a "sandbox",  t. i.e. we have created the conditions for constructing and testing innovative business models, while giving ourselves the opportunity to update the arsenal of regulatory tools. We have implemented a smart electronic licensing tool that allows potential market participants to apply for a license remotely. What are we trying so hard for? I have already mentioned that we are IN FAVOUR of innovations that can give us a favourable direction for the future of finance. On the other hand, in order to have the opportunity to adjust that direction in the desired direction, we must not go from behind and not keep pace with market changes, but at least half a step ahead. This is a prerequisite for managing the challenges that have already been mentioned and are also not mentioned  such as cybersecurity, the threat of international money laundering, or the risks that may arise in the longer term linked to the fragmentation of the financial system and challenges to financial stability  especially if we continue to record the rapid growth of the various categories of crypto-assets. Returning to the global picture: I have mentioned that the European Union has a chance - if it can take advantage of it - to take the role of a 'moderate' foothold between the US and China. Each member of the Community can find its own niche and make its own contribution. I'll admit, I talked so much about Fintech not by accident. We at the Bank of Lithuania believe that the construction of bridges in the FinTech sector can be a niche in Lithuania. We already have work to do in this area. We are actively establishing relations with Asian countries, expanding the geography of interinstitutional cooperation: the path to invest directly in the Chinese capital market has been opened for Lithuanian financial enterprises. We have signed a cooperation agreement with the Chinese banking regulator. This year, we signed an agreement on fintech cooperation with the Central Bank of Singapore. We have also taken on a coordinating role in the development of the joint activities of China and the countries of Central and Eastern Europe in developing an environment conducive to financial technologies. In this and other formats, we present Lithuania to Asian countries as a "gateway" to the European banking and payment market. We have reasons for this kind of introduction. Our licensing regime for fintech companies is not only one of the fastest in Europe, but also one of the most flexible, offering a wide range of business models. In addition, we have opened up the central bank's payment infrastructure to electronic money and payment institutions  through our CENTROlink platform, FinTech companies can access the entire SEPA space directly, without any intermediaries. We can see that the prospect of such access is interesting for third-country companies seeking to enter the European market. Chinese business is also interested in it. We have already granted operating licenses to five FinTech companies in this country. Three more have submitted requests and are currently being evaluated. The flow of contacts indicates that interest is not subsided. Of course, fintech is not the only niche that Lithuania can occupy in search of a place in a new world order. However, it is here that I see a very tangible, achievable and not lacking in potential opportunity. Since I have repeatedly mentioned Asia and China today, I have remembered the old saying of those lands: "the possibility of knocking on the door only once". It is very beautifully complemented by the Proverb of Europeans: "if the opportunity does not knock , install the door". So  let's be vigilant when talking, dreaming, predicting and building the future. When it's knocking  let's open it. And when it doesn't open  let's dare to knock... Thank you for your attention.
