Atskirkime du dalykus, skolinimsi, kada reikia, ir skolint pinig tiksling panaudojim bei ilaidavim. Tai du skirtingi dalykai, a tikrai neatsisakau minties, kad valstybms narms reikia elgtis atsakingai ir pirmiausia tuos skolintus pinigus naudoti ekonominiams suvarymams suvelninti, bet i kitos puss, pinigai turi bti naudojami ir struktrinms reformoms, kurias turi daryti, kad didintum savo konkurencingum ateityje. Mes turime daug sisenjusi problem ir j sprendimas yra privalomas kaip mokiniui nam darb paruoimas. Jei juos paruoi, gali tiktis teigiamo vertinimo, jeigu neparuoi, vlsdsi uodegoje. Ar galime tiktis, kad tas sutarimas anksiau ar vliau bus pasiektas? Jeigu kalbame apie Lietuv, tai ms ekonomin struktra yra domi tuo, kad per kriz pajam nelygyb ir atskirtis kaip tik sumaja. T pastebjome po 2008 met krizs, tai, a manau, vyksta ir dabar. Paskui, kai prasideda vystymasis, vl vyksta tas kreivi isiskyrimas. Bet pajam, turtins padties nelygybi klausimai niekur nenueina nuo darbotvarks. Ar ias problemas padt sprsti bendras Europos Sjungos minimalaus darbo umokesio dydis, bendri mokesiai? Diskusijos iais klausimas vyksta. Kiek to valstybi suvereniteto pavyks perkelti  paneuropin lyg, nuo to priklausys ir diskusij skm.  Grkime gal tada prie ms bank sistemos. Koki j radote ir koki paliekate? Ir jeigu valstybs pozicija pasikeitusi, tai natraliai mes irgi prisitaikome. Tai mums vis laik reikjo aikumo, ta prasme. Ir dabar tas aikumas yra. Jis yra indiferentikas, kitaip sakant, neutralus. Tiesiog pozicija yra tokia, kad negali ignoruoti, kadangi juanis yra rezervin valiuta, traukta  TVF krepel, na, ir viskas tuo pasakyta. Kinija yra antra pagal dyd ekonomika, todl negali to fakto ignoruoti. Politins diskusijos nra tas faktorius,  kur tokia technokratin institucija, kaip euro sistema, Europos Centrinis Bankas ar bet kuris centrinis bankas gali reaguoti arba vaidinti kakok aktyv vaidmen.  Ar yra tikimyb, kad juanio kaip rezervins valiutos reikm dids?  Manyiau, tai yra tiesiogiai susij su Kinijos ekonomikos augimu, todl sakyiau, kad taip.  Ar tai gali kelti pavoj euro kaip rezervins valiutos statusui?  Istorija rodo, kad pasaulins rezervins valiutos gali labai greitai pakeisti savo rol. Galiu pateikti svaro sterling, palyginti su JAV doleriu, pavyzd. Dvideimtojo amiaus pradioje i valiut santykiai buvo visikai kitokie nei amiaus pabaigoje ar dvideimt pirmajame amiuje. A manau, kad ingsniai dl taip vadinamo e. euro yra teisingi, tik iek tiek pavluoti. Galime konstatuoti fakt, kad e. valiutos ar e. pinig srityje Kinija yra gerokai paengusi  priek ir atskirose provincijose t jau naudoja. Kiek Europa sugebs padaryti prover e. valiutos srityje, manau, tai taip pat prisids prie euro kaip valiutos stiprumo. Kol kas a nematau pavojaus euro reikmei tarptautiniuose atsiskaitymuose.  Didiosios Britanijos svaro sterling ir JAV dolerio pavyzdys akivaizdiai rodo, kad valiutos reikm neatsiejama nuo jos valstybs ekonomins ir politins galios. Europos Sjungos pastangos susigrinti gamybinius pajgumus, investuoti  mokslinius tyrimus turti stiprinti ir euro pozicijas. A manau, kad tai yra tiesiogiai susij. Be jokios abejons, ekonomikos dydis ir galia ir neatsiejama nuo valstybs takos ir jos piniginio vieneto reikms tarptautinje erdvje. Mano galva, iuo metu mes susiduriame su keliais vienu metu vykstaniais procesais  dideliu globalizacijos tempu, kuris pastaruoju metu, tiesa, stabteljo, ir nacionaliniais interesais. Taiau mano nuomone, Europa gali bti stipri tik bdama vieninga, stipri valstybi nari laikai jau yra praeityje. Viena Vokietija, viena Pranczija, viena Ispanija kaip atskiros aidjos turi gerokai maesn tarptautins reikms potencial nei Europos Sjunga kaip vieninga ekonomin erdv. Mano nuomone, i Europos Sjungos projekto ilo visi  tiek senosios, tiek naujosios valstybs nars.  Gal galite pasidalinti savo ateities planais? K ketinate veikti iki 2023-j pradios, kai pradsite dirbti Tarptautinio valiutos fondo (TVF) valdyboje, kur atstovausite iaurs ir Baltijos ali regionui?  Kol kas neturiu joki plan. Turiu kelet privai pasilym, bet galioja bendras sistemos atalimo laikotarpis, todl tam tikr laik nordamas sidarbinti turiau gauti Europos Centrinio Banko Etikos komiteto sutikim. Kaip taisykl, maiausiai pus met, o atalimo laikotarpis trunka nuo vieneri iki dvej met, to sutikimo negalima tiktis. Manau, kad artimiausiu metu tiesiog  Taiau finans srities tikriausiai neapleisite?  Labai svarbu utikrinti, kaip a sakau, t degim iki 2023 met. Tarptautiniame valiutos fonde, pasikeitus JAV administracijai, dabar vyksta labai doms dalykai, nuo usidarymo ir TVF reikms mainimo darbotvarks grtama su visikai prieingu poiriu.  Ar manote, kad po ios krizs tiek TVF, tiek kit tarptautini organizacij vaidmuo pasaulio ekonominje ir politinje erdvje stiprs? A tikrai viliuosi ir tikrai to linkiau. Paskutin kriz parod, kad sistemini ir kartu priimam sprendim algoritmas veikia kur kas geriau nei i problem kapstantis atskirai.  Na ir visai pabaigai, ko palinktumte bsimam Lietuvos banko valdybos pirmininkui?  Tiesiog palinkiau komandinio darbo, suvokimo, kad vadovavimas centriniam bankui yra karjeros virn ir viskas, kas bus po to, bus tik jimas nuo kalno. Todl palinkiau pirmiausiai stovti auktai, irti u horizonto, visomis priemonmis kovoti u Lietuvos banko nepriklausomum ir ubaigus darbus oriai pasitraukti. Dkui u pokalb.

Speaking of truths, there is no way to start with something other than the current pandemic situation. The second point is that our financial system is heavily dominated by banks, the capital market as an alternative is sufficiently well developed. The same banking system is very concentrated,constantly recurring problems in the availability of financial services,price problems,I think,at least partially there is such a concentrationsrepresented. - How can the concentration of large banks in the market be reduced? - I think this needs to be seen as a process. We have two systems of central credit unions and 60 credit unions, but somehow in our perspective, the past. Another thing is the capital market. By improving the ability to raise finance and capital in it, we are helping both businesses to obtain new instruments that can raise funds for operations, while on the other hand, financial market participants can raise capital and liquidity through the capital market for their further growth. I believe that there has been a significant increase in controls. - As far as financial technology companies are concerned, is the development of this sector already producing tangible results? - The process is not over yet in order to be able to provide such an assessment, but we increasingly need to think not only about quantitative indicators - the number of new companies or new jobs. Let's just ask those who emit or buy securities what problems they have. Solutions are being sought, for example, in November last year, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Central Banks of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia and the Nordic Investment Bank signed an agreement on strengthening the market for commercial bills of exchange. The issue of financial literacy is very important, the knowledge that there is not only a regulated capital market, but also an unregulated part of it, where there are significantly fewer requirements, there is no need to draw up complex prospectuses. But generations are changing, in business too, people with a new education are coming. It cannot be said that nothing is happening on the capital market, but I would like it to be more accessible and seen as an alternative to the banks. Now, I have to agree, the first option is a loan in a bank. There are a lot of those banks, so you can look for more favourable conditions and, without a doubt, larger businesses do it in the best possible way. By the way, banks strongly compete for good customers. - When you talked about the strengths and weaknesses of the banking system, you did not mention money laundering. You think that's no longer a problem? - No, I believe that the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing is a job that the Bank of Lithuania has to do with other institutions. I would say it was a problem in some other countries and, of course, those splashes are also on us, because we are a country in one region. This must be given special attention at the state level, but this is not our weakness. In understanding these risks, we must, on the one hand, appreciate the rapid growth of the financial sector, and therefore the management and prevention of compliance issues are very important. On the other hand, by understanding these risks, we seek to become a leader in competence in this area. And in this place there is a great example of a private-state partnership - the Center of Excellence for the Prevention of Money Laundering, which was established by the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Lithuania, commercial banks. When we talk about supervision, regulation and things like that, we need to act preventively, not to allow those risks to materialise. If they materialize, it already means that something went wrong, maybe where the control systems did not work, or in the company itself, or the legal base did not require proper control measures, perhaps insufficiently effective things happened in the care, but it is already too late. We must ensure that problems do not arise. - The recent money laundering agents, which mention the large banks of Scandinavia, show that supervisory actions have been delayed. Is the current situation changed? - First of all, these cases have been in other jurisdictions and I would not comment on the supervision of other jurisdictions 4/5 03/08/22, 14:49 G. simkus: we need to strengthen the external financial market participants at the Bank of Lithuania Activity. However, the spurt of fintech companies brings very innovative solutions and is based on them Services. Therefore, it is extremely important that on the maintenance side we are a step ahead. Of course, that's hard to do, but you need to at least keep up and understand how funds move, how services are provided, what solutions applied to prevent risk management. Another thing that digitalization brings, other opportunities for obtaining information appear. Looking ahead, there will be an opportunity to start collecting information on the basis of microdata, which will allow you to react much more effectively in real time to what is happening, intervene in a timely manner and prevent risks. Here's the things of the future, but they're going to have to be done. - Are you talking about Lithuania or more globally? - In this particular case, I have talked about Lithuania, but in reality these initiatives arise at least at European Union level. Of course, other jurisdictions are not compatible with the European Union, but the US, for example, is also implementing similar solutions that allow the collection of microdata from market players. I understand one thing: as part of the banking union, as part of the joint supervisory mechanism, we need to see a common context and fit into the common movement. But this does not mean at all that in individual cases we cannot develop our own solutions, which are based on modern data management, collection, advanced analytics that would allow us to carry out activities more efficiently and qualitatively. - What do you see as your main objectives and challenges in the Lithuanian bank's management? - I have named them both in the Sejm and in the President. The first is the stability and sustainability of the financial system. The second point is the availability of financial services. This issue is repeated over and over again, and I hear that there is a problem, so we must look for ways to respond to the needs of society, because the Bank of Lithuania serves the public interest first and foremost. The third point is a modern and progressive central bank. The fourth point is that discussion and cooperation with other state institutions is more effective, because many of the things I am talking about are joint work between the Bank of Lithuania and other institutions. Without a doubt, it is very important that what we do and communicate is understood by the society for which we work. 5/5

Title: Interview on the portal LRT.lt
text: Interview of G. simkus on the portal LRT.lt Gediminas simkus, Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, is interviewed by journalist Jonas Deveikis. At the beginning of January 2021, Simonas Krpsta, an adviser to President Gitanas Nausda, was named as a candidate for chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania. Later, two months later, your candidacy was also named. Was such an offer a surprise to you? I will say this: I had a very detailed conversation with His Excellency the President in the summer of last year, before I was appointed as a member of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania. Then the conversation was long. I had to present how I understand the economy, the financial sector, how I imagine the Bank of Lithuania. I think that was the beginning of that journey that brought me to this position. Did you hesitate for a long time when you heard the offer? I have been working in the banking sector for almost 20 years. During this time, I have gone through various stages, from a simple economist to a consistently climbing career ladder to the top. I myself have asked myself what would be the alternative to say no, when I know for sure what a central bank is, and I can certainly not only work for the Bank of Lithuania and the people of Lithuania, but also change what the Bank of Lithuania is doing to how, in my opinion, it should be in order to serve the public good to the maximum. One of the objectives you have identified is to ensure access to financial services. In recent years, the number of bank branches in the regions has decreased, and cash transactions have become more expensive. How will you deal with this problem? Will you teach pensioners how to use a computer, or maybe other state institutions, such as Lithuanian Post, could serve customers? If there had been a magic bullet that could solve this problem, it would have been used long ago. One side of the coin is that the financial sector and individual participants seek to optimize their network in order to stay competitive. The other side of the coin is that these changes have consequences for people whose regions bank branches are leaving or ATMs are being closed. This forces people to change habits and causes discontent. This is also shown by the polls. The (un)availability of cash is identified as a problem by almost one fifth of the population, which is almost the largest share in the entire European Union (EU). It is necessary to note that financial literacy is very important. Cash is not the only means of payment, so you need to know the possibilities. And the last thing is that both the executive authorities and the Bank of Lithuania have made a huge contribution to bringing fintech companies to Lithuania. We have over 100 electronic money payment institutions that provide a wide range of services. In this cocktail we need to find the best combination. However, fintech companies also need to provide services that, by their kindness, overtake the old services. There is more than one way to deal with this problem, but to come from my side and say that we are doing this would not be very responsible. I believe that technological progress must not leave any group of society behind it, and our society consists of various social groups. But what would you suggest you do to a 70-year-old person who lives in the village, and there is no bank branch nearby, you did not answer. A man who lives in the village and who is 70 years old has never been around and has not had a bank branch. It is therefore necessary to agree on to the public what the minimum requirements are and what we call the availability of cash. Let's think about what we can put on the table, and then let's talk. When the vote on your candidacy took place, the members of the Seimas pointed out that both in 2011 and in 2016, parliamentarians presented the same problems to the future Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania  bank rates, high interest rates, access to financing for small and medium-sized businesses. 10 years have passed and the same problems are mentioned again. Why have they not been resolved so far? I don't want to appreciate what it was like before I became chairman of the bank's board of directors. I look to the future and direct my actions there. In my opinion, there have been strong changes in the market, some of the previously existing banks have left the market, market concentration has increased, but at the same time the cooperative banking sector has strengthened, and new entrants have emerged, including banks. In Lithuania, there are two central credit unions with 60 credit unions that cover the whole of Lithuania and the regions, there are 11 banks and specialized banks, 6 foreign bank branches operating in the country. I think during those years, efforts have been made to attract foreign market participants. We could strengthen the already existing market players, who are too small. Credit unions have also strengthened significantly in recent years and, looking to the future, this can be a promising area where regional market participants could become at the national level. A very important service of banks is a home loan. The interest rates offered by credit unions on a home loan are often higher than those offered by the major national banks. Do you imagine that people would take home loans from credit unions more often in the future? I can fully imagine. Here you need to ask why in credit unions the interest rate on housing loans is higher than in ordinary retail banks. This may also be due to the fact that the interest rates on deposits and the cost of financial resources in credit unions are higher. Credit unions are faced with more complex options for raising capital. They develop their banking activities in a region with a specific market. Let us also not forget that the activities of credit unions are based on social principles. But could credit unions provide the competitive home loans that the country's major banks offer? A good customer can and I think they can in the future. And you yourself, as a consumer, are satisfied with banking services, rates? I once had a very large number of bank accounts, but at one time I closed all the accounts and stayed in one bank. I have no complaints with the bank as a financial service provider. But I live in the city, my access to financial services is different than that of the people who live in Jiezne. If we are talking about service rates, it was once a very acute problem for individuals. Then the basket of payment services was established and the basic price was set. This problem was answered a few years ago. Therefore, as an individual, I have no complaints, and I do not conduct business. In order to increase competition between banks, you propose to strengthen credit unions, existing market participants. And would it be possible to bring a large bank to Lithuania in five years, which would be engaged in retail banking? After all, the profit margin in the sector is such that banks do not have to complain. Large banks require volumes of activity. If we tell the big players in the European market that they can earn some millions of euros in this market, they may not be interested, because the volume of activity will be too small. They need to enter the market, start operations from the beginning, so the amount of profit may not satisfy them. This is one of the reasons why several market participants have emerged. Another option is for banks operating abroad to acquire here an already operating market participant with all the infrastructure. Such a prospect is possible. However, let us not forget that we are in a single market where goods and services move freely. Financial market participants licensed in Lithuania can and do provide financial services in other countries. Therefore, it is necessary to ask how to attract institutions operating in other countries to provide services in Lithuania without establishing a subsidiary, a branch of a foreign bank. Do you know a person living in Lithuania who would have taken out a loan from a bank abroad to buy an apartment in Lithuania? I don't know them personally, but I'm sure there's more than one of them. The Bank of Lithuania forecasts economic growth of 2.9 per cent this year and 5.1 per cent in 2022. Is it possible to say that for the next two years it is not worth fearing about the economic situation in the country? I don't like the word "to fear." We need to be rational about what is. Lockdown restrictions are loosening, but the virus hasn't gone anywhere. I would therefore urge everyone to act responsibly. Having said this, it can be added that Lithuania coped well with the economic shock caused by the virus. The country's economic downturn was one of the lowest in the EU, but it also led to one of the largest debt increases. Yes, we are forecasting a growth of 2.9% this year, but it is not very correct to talk about a specific estimate, because we can see that the lockdown can be extended. However, it is worth noting that pessimistic, basic and optimistic scenarios are on positive territory. So we can see that this year we will have economic growth and recovery to pre-crisis levels. Last year, the number of bankruptcies was perhaps the lowest in the last 5 years. Can the number of bankruptcies be expected to increase in the near future? I do not think that we will see a huge jump in the number of bankruptcies, although there will certainly be some. I would also like to point out that state aid has made it possible to postpone what might have happened inevitably. During the crisis, we had fewer bankruptcies than in the good times. As far as bankruptcies are concerned, I would not say that this will be a huge danger to our economy, and the greatest likelihood of bankruptcies will be where business sectors have faced the greatest lockdown restrictions. And how do you assess business support measures? If you were a representative of small or medium-sized businesses, would the support mechanisms satisfy you? The latest economic aid measures are aimed at those sectors that have suffered the most. Although one can argue about the criteria themselves, I welcome this. The level of public debt reached 47.3% of the country's GDP in 2020, and this year it will exceed the 50% threshold. Some economists say: let's borrow more because it's cheap. Can the state borrow even more? Although historically this is the highest level of debt for Lithuania, it is not much in the EU context. Here it is worth highlighting not the size itself, but what would have happened if certain measures had not been taken, which led to an increase in public debt. Would this not have made the public debt even bigger later, because businesses would have collapsed, people would have lost their jobs, they would have to pay benefits. At the moment, it is important to talk about a plan to manage public debt, financial prospects and recovery funds. They must be used as closely as possible, investing in digital, green technologies, in measures that will ensure high value-added products. And could we afford to increase the debt even more? There are small euro area countries that have a higher debt than Lithuania. As a result, the public debt, if necessary, could increase and a catastrophe would not occur. But it's not right to think that way. It is necessary to think, not what it would be like if the debt increased even more, but why it increases and how we use the funds that lead to an increase in debt. The European Commission (EC) proposes that Lithuania should increase the working age to 72 years by 2040. What would be your position on this? The pension system is designed to ensure that in old age people receive a dignified income. We have a 3-pillar pension system. In the first pillar, pensions are paid from the social security contributions collected. The amount of contributions may depend on the number of people employed, on the amount of contributions paid, on the number of people who are paid pensions. The EC's proposal concerns only the last part , the number of people in retirement, but there are other components of the pension. However, if the number of people in work remains the same, social security contributions will remain the same and the number of pensioners increases, something will have to change. Either pensions will remain at a similar level, or something will have to change. That is why I believe that the second tier plays an important role here. I know that not all economists agree with this position, but it is the additional accumulation that creates another reserve that can be brought to old age. As the calculations show, if a person accumulates for decades, it will be a strong help in retirement. However, is the European Commission's proposal to increase the length of working age the best way to maintain the rate of change at retirement age? The best thing is to return the emigrated citizens of our country to Lithuania. Canada's central bank, which met last week, said it was going to raise the base rate earlier than planned. Is there a chance of seeing a rising base rate in the euro area in a few years? Everything will depend on the economic situation. The monetary policy of the European Central Bank is responsive to the available information and forecasts. If information changes and economic data show that the economy is recovering and inflation is returning to a sustainable path, then, of course, this is possible. Does this mean that people with a home loan should stumble that the era of low interest rates will not last long and will have to pay more for a home loan? Fortunately, we have responsible lending provisions in Lithuania. This is our success story and many states are trying to copy us. There are several parameters in those provisions: the ratio of the value of the loan to the value of real estate, the ratio of the loan payment in comparison with the total income, and the interest rate jump. This means that the ratio of the loan instalment to the income must be maintained by the person even in the event of a 5 percentage point increase in the interest rate. Consequently, the borrower's ability to repay the loan is checked by borrowing and it is assessed whether he will be able to repay the loan if the interest rate increases by 5 percentage points. Currently, the real estate market in the capital is very active. Would you yourself now buy an apartment in Vilnius for life? I would buy an apartment for life both at this time, and 5 years ago, and after 5 years. When you decide to buy a home for life, it's not an investment, but a cost, since the alternative would be renting or living with your parents. The subtext of your question concerns prices  whether they are currently high or low. I knew very good economists who waited for the price drop and bought a home at the very peak of prices. Therefore, let us not speculate. What about investing or buying? Investing in real estate is risky. We often think we understand the real estate market, just like we all think we're good basketball coaches. In fact, while some may disagree, it's a risky investment. In the spring, we saw a new launch of the Ignitis group of companies in the financial markets. On Wednesday, the Government agreed to turn 4 state-owned enterprises into joint-stock companies. Would you agree that more public undertakings should end up in the financial markets? The internal capital market needs to be strengthened and, in my opinion, at least some of the public undertakings could enter the market and thus raise capital and invigorate the internal capital market. In addition, we are talking about increasing competition in the banking sector, which could be an alternative to bank financing. The Ministry of Finance has set up a working group on the review of tax breaks to make recommendations on how the country's tax system should be changed. The proposals are promised to be implemented in 2023. In your opinion, what kind of tax reform would be needed Lithuania? Lithuania needs systemic tax reform. When some come and fix one thing, then others come, the whole is gone in the tax system. We have one of the smallest redistributions of state income through the budget, we have a large VAT gap, we have a 'livestock farm', we have very different social security contributions, we have a complex accounting system. We also have tax innovations made in the previous term, which looked good when taxes were rising as incomes grew. But if taxes were rising as the company grew, it means that Steve Jobs wouldn't have grown Apple in The United States and would have stayed in the garage because taxes would have been lower. I certainly support the review of tax breaks. This is a good start, but we need to move on to changing the system and ask what our state's obligations are, how much we can collect in the budget so that we can finance the services with which we are satisfied. What do you like to do in your free time, do you have time for this at the moment? There's not much free time at the moment. My free time is devoted to the family. I'm raising my daughter, and I'm paying all my attention to her. Maybe you're watching movies or reading books? The latest series I reviewed was Sharp Objects. I could definitely recommend it. And the latest fiction book I read was about the life of singer Freddie Mercury. What qualities do you think a manager needs? The leader must be able to hear, be able to ask a question and wait for the answer "why". You have to have the courage to make decisions about when they need to be made. If you had a magic wand and could change one thing, what would it be? I would change the Lithuanian way and one of its features. We have a lot of advice for others, for ourselves, but we get stuck in implementing them. I would therefore like us to clearly define where we would like to be and to go there.

Turime ir prajusios kadencijos metu padaryt mokesi inovacij, kurios atrod neblogos, kada augant pajamoms didja mokesiai. Bet jei augant monei didja mokesiai, tai reikia, kad Steve'as Jobsas Apple nebt augins Lietuvoje ir bt liks garae, nes mokesiai bt buv maesni. Tikrai palaikau mokesi lengvat perir. Tai gera pradia, bet reikia pereiti  sistemos keitim ir klausti, kokie yra ms valstybs sipareigojimai, kiek mes galime surinkti  biudet, kad galtume finansuoti paslaugas, kuriomis btume patenkinti. K mgstate veikti laisvalaikiu, ar tam iuo metu turite laiko? Laisvalaikio iuo metu nelabai ir lik. Mano laisvalaikis yra skiriamas eimai. Auginu dukrel, jai ir skiriu vis dmes. Galbt filmus irite ar knygas skaitote? Naujausias serialas, kur perirjau, buvo Sharp Objects. Tikrai galiau rekomenduoti. O naujausia perskaityta groin knyga buvo apie dainininko Freddie Mercury gyvenim. Kaip manote, koki savybi reikia vadovui? Vadovas turi mokti girdti, mokti uduoti klausim ir ilaukti atsakymo kodl. Turi turti drsos priimti sprendimus, kada juos reikia priimti. Jeigu turtumte burt lazdel ir galtumte pakeisti vien dalyk, kas tai bt? Pakeisiau lietuvik bd ir vien jo ypatyb. Mes turime labai daug patarim kitiems, sau, taiau ustringame juos gyvendindami. Todl noriau, kad aikiai apsibrtume, kur nortume bti, ir ten nukeliautume.

Title: Speech at Conference Post-Pandemic Economic Recovery: Realities and Perspectives
text: 03/08/22 , 14:30 ffl'I:) LI.ETUVQS B,AN KAS Speech by Gediminas imkus I Bank of Lithuania Speechby GediminasSimkusat Conference"PostPandemicEconomicRecovery:Realitiesand Perspectives" 2021-06-04 SpeechbyGediminasSimkus,Chairmanof the Boardof the Bankof Lithuania,at high-level conference,,Post-pandemiceconomicrecovery: realitiesand perspectives"on 4 June 2021. CHECK AGAINST DELIVERY Dear Governors , Central Bankers and Colleagues, It is a great honour to address you on this momentous occasion . The National Bank of Moldova (NBM) is currently celebrating its 30th anniversary . Over the past three decades, the NBM has achieved a great deal: from banking sector rehabilitation to delivering on price and financial sector stability - and much besides. m1of 1 I wish to highlight, if I may, the word "maturity" . The NBM has matured into a central bank with solid capacity and expertise, resilient governance, autonomy, policy credibility and a strong standing within the international central banking community. This maturity is reflected in the topic chosen for our first session today - the role of central banks in the post-pandemic recovery. This is a topic of strategic importance and long time horizon. It is only fitting that we are having this discussion on such a notable occasion. My brief intervention today will focus on two groups : first, advanced economy central banks, and second, central banks in the emerging markets . Let me begin with the advanced world. 1/4 03/08/22, 14:30 Speechby GediminasSimkusI Bankof Lithuania A strong fiscal impulse, alongside a highly successful vaccination campaign, will put the US economy above its potential already this year. The euro area will continue to operate with a negative output gap. By 2022, it is very likely that the US will have caught up with its pre-pandemic growth trend. There is little chance of that happening in the euro area in the foreseeable future. A heated debate is taking place on the possibility of the US experiencing a surge of inflation. Such an eventuality would not allow for synchronised tightening across the advanced economies. Managing such desynchronisation may prove to be challenging. At the same time, we should not rush to conclusions. The environment in which monetary policy operates has changed in recent years. The natural real rate of interest has declined to O% or even lower over the past two decades in both the US and Europe. Phillips curves have become considerably flatter in this period. Several structural factors underlie this diminished relation between inflation and economic activity. The first is globalisation, which has limited inflation in traded goods - and even certain services. A second factor is automation, which, through productivity gains, has kept higher wages from being passed through to prices. Moreover, research shows that real equilibrium rates tend to fall following pandemics. The pandemic will likely reinforce "secular stagnation" trends, magnifying the savings absorption problem and its effects on the persistently low inflation. In the euro area, the aggregate unemployment rate is higher compared to the US or Japan. Current tendencies in the labour market - such as the emergence of the gig economy and the absence of stronger labour unions - are leading to a diminishing power of European labour. This in turn makes it increasingly difficult to build wage pressures that could raise inflation. The evidence we have on the table, then, indicates that a sustained surge of inflation is an unlikely event - be it in the US, Europe or elsewhere. For the same reason that inflation did not drop significantly when output gaps were large and negative during the global financial crisis, inflation is unlikely to increase to worrisome levels now. Of course, centrals banks need to stay vigilant and closely monitor inflation developments, so that sudden reactionary policy does not put the brakes on economic recovery. In light of all this, the implications of low natural real interest rates will remain a first-order issue for advanced economy central banks in the post-pandemic period. 2/4 03/08/22, 14:30 Speechby GediminasSimkusI Bankof Lithuania Fiscal policy is the first tool in line, along with structural reforms, to affect conditions shaping the current low interest rate environment. Here I would recall the well-known maxim: monetary policy cannot be the only game in town. Indeed, one explanation for the superior inflation performance of the US relative to the euro area over the recent decade is the greater alignment of monetary and fiscal policies in the former. Accordingly, the key risk in the post-pandemic period is that poor coordination between monetary and fiscal policy leads to a continued and pronounced undershooting of the inflation objective. But central banks can also play their part. This is why the decline in the natural real interest rate continues to be a central topic in our ECB strategy review. The review was postponed due to the pandemic and is now set to conclude in the second half of 2021. Our reaction function will likely evolve on the basis of this review exercise. For instance, a stronger emphasis on the symmetry in our inflation target is vital given the new realities. However, that step might not suffice to convince markets and agents in the real economy that we are serious about reaching the inflation target. Allowing for a period of above-target inflation to compensate for a sustained undershoot might be an additional tool to increase inflation expectations. Crucially, we must maintain our flexibility in order to ensure that we continue to effectively carry out our mandate. Beyond monetary policy, the importance of macroprudential policy will only grow in the low interest rate environment - especially considering the current level of monetary accommodation and the possible side effects of the non-standard measures. The time is coming when policy-makers will need to consider tightening selected macroprudential policy tools to tackle pockets of elevated vulnerability. For instance, throughout the COVID-19 crisis the demand for housing continued to increase in many countries, drawing attention to risks in the residential real estate sector. These include a possible house price overvaluation, elevated household indebtedness and high residential real estate exposures of banks. Let me now turn to the emerging markets. During the peak of the pandemic crisis, capital outflows from emerging market economies (EMEs) were unprecedented in scale and speed - but also short-lived. EMEs, including Moldova, shed their "fear of floating" and allowed the exchange rate to move and absorb the shock. In sharp contrast to previous crises a full one-third of EMEs have employed quantitative easing (QE). In the past, EMEs generally tightened monetary policy to avoid rapid capital outflows and the inflationary effect of exchange rate depreciations. The current crisis has seen EME policy reaction being more in line with that of 3/4 03/08/22, 14:30 Speechby GediminasSimkusI Bankof Lithuania advances economies, with QE being launched even before reaching the zero lower bound on policy rates. Financial markets mostly responded favourably to the QE announcements. Central banks successfully communicated that they stood behind their sovereign should fiscal expansion undermine investor confidence. Long-term interest rates decreased in response, while exchange rates did not move significantly. How can we explain this EME resilience? Of course, large-scale injections of new liquidity by the Fed and other systemic central banks have eased global financial conditions and redirected investors to EMEs in the quest for better-yielding asset classes. Let us not underestimate, however, the progress achieved by the EMEs themselves. In recent years, a number of EMEs have strengthened their monetary policy frameworks, anchored inflation expectations and further developed local currency sovereign debt markets. This enabled them to step into terra incognito with asset purchases when the crisis hit. Such experience confirms that strong fundamentals constitute the first line of defence for EME central banks against potential shocks. As the emerging market sell-off in 2018 or the 2013 taper tantrum tells us, capital flows to EMEs are vulnerable to advanced economy central bank policy movements, particularly by the US FED. Therefore, now is the time for EMEs to further strengthen their monetary policy frameworks - and build on their hard-won monetary policy independence. International institutions, such as the IMF, are there to assist countries through programmes or capacitydevelopment IMF programmes for emerging markets often stress the need to safeguard central bank independence and strengthen monetary policy frameworks, which can substantially support EMEs under stress. Moving forward, we can see the contours of what needs to be done to prepare for the post-pandemic economy. But this brave new world may look different than we currently imagine. Some have suggested that we are entering uncharted waters, which may require novel ideas and bold action. I thus hope that we can return to this topic and continue our dialogue. Meanwhile, I wish you an enlightening and enjoyable conference. Economic analY.sisand Q[Qjections. International relations. COVID-19 4/4

Title: AMLA is an essential step towards transforming and enhancing AML/CFT supervision
text: AMLA is an essential step towards transforming and enhancing AML/CFT supervision Media Speeches, interviews, presentations RSS Newsletter 2022-02-28 Article by Gediminas Simkus, Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania for the Eurofi Magazine. Massive technological innovation is rapidly changing the face of the financial sector. Cross-border payments these days can be made instantaneously any time of the day and week, with the number of payment providers and the overall complexity of the financial system growing. The Financial Action Task Force reports that multiple jurisdictions are facing increased vulnerabilities, particularly due to a rise in remote transactions. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the pace of change in customers financial patterns - more people work from home and conduct more online transactions than ever before. With such a transformation taking place, sound, prudent and accurate AML/CFT procedures must be a top priority for financial market participants. Even though AML frameworks are improving, substantial amounts of money involved in suspect financial activity are still being detected. Europol assesses the annual cost of money-laundering to the European economy at well over 100 billion EUR. Therefore the EU Member-States must take action. Besides efforts to improve efficiency of the national AML/CFT frameworks, a further push is needed to implement more uniform AML supervision across the EU Member-States and to establish an effective EU AML Authority (AMLA). Money-laundering and terrorism-financing activities are not contained within national borders. Accordingly, a truly effective framework for AML/CFT must be international. Completing the Single Market for services requires a well-functioning financial sector, and a well- functioning financial sector requires AML/CFT compliance at the very heart of financial companies, with uniform rules for compliance across the EU. To ensure this, we need a harmonized AML/CFT supervision framework. Currently, AML/CFT regulatory and supervisory system is too country-centric and therefore application of the rules for compliance vary depending on the country. The recent proposal of the Commission introduces a Single Rulebook for preventing the financial system from being used for the purposes of money-laundering or financing terrorism. Such a Single Rulebook in place at the EU level will stop regulatory arbitrage and provide a basis for an effective supervisory practises. Furthermore, the Commission proposes to expand the rules against anti-money-laundering or terrorism financing regarding crypto-assets and related service providers - a crucial step, given the mounting evidence from research of illegal activities involving such assets. At the center of such an EU-wide supervisory framework for AML and CFT should be a competent AMLA. A capable AMLA has the potential to improve the resilience of the European financial system, reduce the likelihood of systemic errors, and allow individual cases to be handled with greater efficiency. To this end, it must be ensured that AMLA has a broad mandate, covering a range of players in the financial sector, and its staff have thorough knowledge in all areas of financial services. In addition, there must be clear and objective criteria for determining which institutions fall under AMLAs direct supervision, ensuring an appropriate balance between AMLA and national AML/CFT supervisors, in both the overall supervisory framework and the day-to-day operations. Last but not least, it is of utmost importance for AMLA to have a good overview and knowledge of the EU Member States1 markets, as well as to promote the convergence of supervisory practices. Therefore, at least one entity per Member State should fall under direct AMLA supervision. AMLA should work in close cooperation not only with national AML/CFT supervisors, but also with other institutions - ESAs, for example - to ensure the flow of all necessary information. Currently, we lack a well-defined common structure to support such cooperation at the EU level. This shortage of common tools and resources leads to situations where too few cross-border joint analyses by AML/CFT and non-AML/CFT supervisors are carried out, hindering the capacity to detect money-laundering and terrorism financing early on. Creating an EU-wide AML/CFT data hub, administered by AMLA, that integrates data from all sides is vital, as access to reliable, accurate, detailed and real-time data is crucial for an effective AMLA. Building up an EU-wide AML/CFT framework with an AMLA at the center of it is not an easy feat. However, we are sure to succeed, as we start from vast experiences of AML/CFT coordination at the national level and recognize prevention of money-laundering and terrorism financing as our top priority. Title: Completing the Banking Union is a necessary step towards ending ring-fencing
text: Completing the Banking Union is a necessary step towards ending ring-fencing Media Speeches, interviews, presentations RSS Newsletter 2022-02-28 Article by Gediminas Simkus, Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania for the Eurofi Magazine. The benefits of cross-border banking are indisputable -- it allows for economies of scale and geographic diversification, reduces bank exposure to negative shocks through better risk sharing, and enables a more efficient allocation of resources. So-called ring- fencing practices, such as application of capital and liquidity requirements on banks limiting activities to national boundaries, hinder the deepening of the single banking market. Typically, ring- fencing evolves as a result of countries concerns about financial stability. The resulting fragmentation comes at a cost for both the efficiency of the financial system and the banks themselves. While the issue of ring-fencing should be resolved, developing pan-European banks should not come at the expense of host jurisdictions. Only completing and expanding the Banking Union, and complementing it with a deep and well-integrated Capital Markets Union, would sufficiently reduce the risks that can presently be addressed only by domestic ring-fencing. First, the European Deposit Insurance Scheme (EDIS) - the third pillar of the Banking Union - should be established and become fully operational. For host countries, a fully-fledged EDIS is crucial. A hybrid model, where EDIS only comes in once national depositor protection tools are depleted, is not an adequate compromise. As banks become larger, we need correspondingly stronger safeguards. Assume that a consolidated transnational bank (for which the prudential requirements are applied on a group level only) fails and the host country has to compensate the depositors of its domestic subsidiary. Local taxpayers exposure to the risk of losses can be substantially reduced only with a fully-fledged EDIS in place. Furthermore, a fully-fledged EDIS is necessary to remove present risks of transforming subsidiaries into branches. Home countries as well as hosts face downside financial stability risks, because the home country might be unable to cover depositor claims of the large banks in other Member States. Such risks are even more pronounced when a large entity makes its headquarters in a small home jurisdiction. As occurred in one case in the EU, if a banks asset portfolio becomes three times larger than the GDP of the home nation, the stakes on EDIS rise. Second, further efforts should be taken to expand the Banking Union beyond the euro-area. This is important for countries where a substantial share of the banking sector is foreign-owned, primarily by non-euro area entities. For example, the parent companies of many of the largest banks in the Baltic States are not supervised by the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM). A Banking Union which spans beyond the euro-area would solve this issue. We should therefore look for ways to encourage the non- euro area countries to joining the Banking Union through the close cooperation regime by emphasizing the benefits of the SSM supervisory expertise, information-sharing, and efficiencies arising when the home and the host jurisdictions make collective decisions. Finally, it must be noted that while the completion of the Banking Union with a fully-fledged EDIS and establishing a pan-European Banking Union are both key in curtailing ring-fencing practices, these alone are not enough. For a truly integrated European banking market, we also need a deep and well-functioning Capital Markets Union. Research shows that while risk is efficiently shared in a banking union when economies are hit with demand shocks, a capital markets union is necessary to help absorb supply-side shocks. Without security market integration complementing banking activities, as well as a higher level of harmonization of national insolvency and taxation regimes among the European Union member states, cross-border banking will remain hindered. Removing the non-prudential barriers to cross-border banking will take time and determination. Member States need to agree on how to collect taxes on cross-border investments and establish unified definitions of the underlying tax base for banks. Furthermore, insolvency law should be harmonized to make outcomes of insolvency procedures more predictable. For this reason, we have to take a long-term view and aim to reform these specific topics which create obstacles to pan-European activities. An incomplete Banking Union is the main reason behind the low levels of cross-border consolidation in the European banking sector. Thus, a complete and expanded Banking Union, complemented by a well-functioning Capital Markets Union, should allow us to suspend ring-fencing practices and unlock the full potential of Europe-wide banking. Supervision of financial market participants

Title: An open strategic autonomy must be ensured in the EUs financial sector
text: An open strategic autonomy must be ensured in the EUs financial sector Media Speeches, interviews, presentations 2022-09-07 RSS Newsletter Print Article by Gediminas Simkus, Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, for the Eurofi Views Magazine. Initially limited to matters of defense, the concept of strategic autonomy has in the past years found echoes in all EU policies. We are moving towards less trade with geopolitically more risky countries, with a goal of greater independence in the production of essential goods and digital sovereignty. At the same time, the EU strives for deeper integration and must avoid protectionism, aiming for an open strategic autonomy. According to the European Commission, the EU should be open where we can, but autonomous where we must. The financial sector is one of the key areas in which such an open strategic autonomy must be ensured. Financial and real economy sectors go hand in hand, and without fostering autonomy in both, the macroeconomic stability and resilience of the EU cannot be ensured. Achieving this aim requires a complex dance of dependencies and capabilities. The EUs financial sector is large and very open internationally. This openness spurs competition; however, to date, the European financing model is still heavily skewed towards bank financing. Too few European companies go public, and when they do, they tend to use third-country exchanges to raise funding. Excessive reliance on third-country critical service providers, such as central counterparties clearing derivatives and third-country digital technologies, creates financial stability risks in times of market disruption. We must therefore take the necessary steps to tackle such dependencies. In this pursuit, however, we must not simply replace one dependency with another. We should avoid the pitfalls of picking national or binational winners, focusing on national goals rather than European ones, and setting standards in areas where we are not technologically competitive. Let me expand on this idea. While one could see a point in cautioning that if we dont build our own champions in all areas - digital, artificial intelligence - our choices will be dictated by others1, we cannot proceed by simply picking national champions and allowing them to compete in strategically sensitive sectors internationally. Doing so would stifle innovation and put the SMEs from smaller EU member states at a disadvantage, as they would not be able to benefit from customized innovative products. Instead of picking champions, the EU should identify key European eco-systems that deserve support and foster deeper EU-wide cooperation. Horizontal rather than vertical policies could be pursued, with vertical policies embraced only where they contribute to the EU-wide strategic autonomy without undermining the level playing field. While completion of the Banking Union and the deepening of the Capital Markets Union are crucial, harmonization of the legislation with regards to insolvency and taxation is of prime importance too. To this end, we welcome plans of the European Commission to present Customs and Taxation as well as further Capital Markets packages this winter. The EUs open strategic autonomy is inseparable from the promotion of financial innovation supporting the EUs climate and digital transitions. The EUs role as a global standard-setter can be a key element in the EU toolbox to promote this. Nevertheless, we cannot just set the rules and be the referee; we need to be players as well in order to credibly shape global standards. Therefore, the EU can only use its standard-setting power in areas where it is technologically prominent and competitive. One such area is data collection, management, and protection. Through such initiatives as the European Single Access Point as an EU-wide data powerhouse with sustainability data on European companies, or the creation of the consolidated tape for transactions taking place on trading platforms across the EU, European companies would be made more visible, accessible, and comparable. Combined with an interconnected and open technology sector in Europe, such initiatives would provide the continent with a strong position to set global standards and promote European values, as well as to maintain and expand Europes economy. The past few years have witnessed a need to strike an appropriate balance between achieving economic and financial autonomy on the one hand and maintaining openness and global cooperation with like-minded partners to reap the potential benefits thereof, on the other. The EU must continue working to achieve an open and stable international economic ecosystem against the background of profound changes to the global economic and geopolitical order. Experience has shown that coping with such changes takes time, leadership, and stamina. Let us thus follow the tried and true approach of not letting a good crisis go to waste and institutionalize our long-term strategies. 1 Interview with French President Emmanuel Macron at the Radio France International, September 2019.

Title: Advancing EUs open strategic autonomy best response to geopolitical challenges
text: Advancing Ells open strategic autonomy best response to geopolitical challenges Media Speeches, interviews, presentations 2022 10 17 RSS Newsletter Print Article by Gediminas Simkus, Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, for the OMFIF Autumn Bulletin 2022. Russias brutal war against Ukraine has created new geopolitical and economic challenges with many uncertainties, high energy prices, risks to the energy supply, slowing growth and rising inflation. There is a move towards less trade with geopolitically more risky countries, aimed at greater independence in the production of essential goods, more secure provision of essential services and enhanced digital sovereignty. The concept of strategic autonomy is gaining traction in all European Union policy arenas. As the EU strives for reduced dependencies on third parties, together with a deeper integration among its members, it must avoid protectionism and aim for an open strategic autonomy. The financial sector is one of the key areas in which such an open strategic autonomy must be ensured. The EUs financial sector is very open internationally. Openness spurs competition. However, Europes financing model is still heavily skewed towards bank financing. Too few European companies go public and capital markets in many member states are underdeveloped. Excessive reliance on third-country critical service providers, such as central counterparties clearing derivatives and third-country digital technologies, creates risk in times of market disruption. Steps must be taken to tackle such vulnerabilities. To this end, there is a compelling need to complete the capital markets union, as one of the prerequisites for achieving European strategic autonomy in the financial sector. A deep and complete CMU is not a goal in itself but rather a vital element in delivering on the key economic policy objectives of the post-pandemic recovery and overcoming economic challenges related to the increasingly complex geopolitical situation. It will also help ensure that the transition towards both a more digital and more sustainable economy is a success. Well-developed capital markets can offer an attractive alternative for firms operating in bank- based financial structures. Small- and medium-sized enterprises in countries where capital markets are less developed cannot access capital from developed markets unless they are business prodigies. SMEs therefore have to rely on bank funding. It is no secret that banks are less eager to finance investments directed towards innovative technologies, including innovative green technologies. The current geopolitical situation highlights that the only sustainable way to reduce our reliance on imported fossil fuels is to move fast with the green transition. Lithuania started shifting away from Russias market after the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and invested in the development of critical energy infrastructure, namely the Klaipeda liquid natural gas terminal. This allowed Lithuania to completely stop imports of Russian gas in response to Moscows invasion of Ukraine. However, Lithuania will only achieve full energy independence when it successfully boosts the capacity of local green energy production. This transition will be neither fast nor smooth without an environment in which investments towards innovative green technologies are encouraged. Lithuania must boost the growth of the entire financial sector by increasing competition and access to services, as well as strengthening the capital market, thereby creating high added value for citizens, businesses and the economy in general. The development of local and regional capital markets is only the first step towards deeper European cross-border capital markets. Without the free flow of capital and savings across EU member states, efforts to foster green innovation and Europes resilience to future shocks will only yield limited results. Any actions towards deeper EU integration should be horizontal and broad rather than national or regional. Ensuring Europes strategic autonomy in the financial sector requires strong political support and a willingness to make EU-level reforms on sensitive issues such as taxation and insolvency. Open economies always gain when regulation is harmonised and calibrated equally. At the same time, smaller economies tend to lose out when the national champions are chosen to compete in strategically sensitive sectors internationally, because then possibilities for product customisation become limited. A deep single market for capital, complemented by the integration of banking markets, is of utmost importance if the EU is serious about the acceleration of economic growth and strategic autonomy. However, there must be an appropriate balance between achieving such economic and financial autonomy, on the one hand, and maintaining openness and global co- operation with like-minded partners to reap the potential benefits, on the other. The EU must continue working with its strategic partners to achieve an open and stable international economic ecosystem against the background of profound changes to the global order. Experience has shown that coping with such changes takes time, leadership and stamina. The EUs role as a global standard setter is a key part of its toolbox as it promotes global co- operation based on European values. Data collection, management and protection is one such area where the EU could demonstrate its prominence. Through such initiatives as the European Single Access Point or the creation of the consolidated tape for transactions taking place on trading platforms across the EU, European companies will be made more visible, accessible and comparable. Combined with an interconnected and open technology sector in Europe, such initiatives will provide the continent with a strong foundation on which to set global standards, as well as to maintain and expand Europes economy. Advancing the EUs open strategic autonomy in the financial sector is key if Europe is to overcome challenges, meet its financing needs in the long term and ensure the prosperity of the continents economy. With joint effort and innovative thinking, Europe will be able to successfully adjust to the new geopolitical reality. There is no other choice.

Title: Speech by G. imkus at the Bank of Lithuania Real Estate Conference
text: Speech by G. simkus at the Bank of Lithuania Real Estate Conference For media Languages, interviews, presentations RSS News subscription Print 2022-11-17 Welcome speech by Gediminas simkus, Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, at the tenth annual real estate conference of the Bank of Lithuania. This text is not a transcript of the language. Good morning, dear real estate experts, viewers of the broadcast of the event, dear colleagues! I am delighted with this  anniversary  centenary year of the Bank of Lithuania by congratulating you, who also gathered for the anniversary  the tenth  1 of 1 The Real Estate Conference of the Bank of Lithuania. Despite all the uncertainties, I could almost bet that there would be the eleventh too. The full hall and the record number of registered "remote" participants confirm that in a decade the event not only did not get bored, did not breathe and did not live, but even became even more relevant, necessary and, I very much hope, more useful. It is likely that the growing popularity of the event is also fueled by circumstances. The last few years have been extremely dynamic in the real estate (RE) market. And not only that  it's still unique in something. For example, when we met two years ago, we had a virtual discussion about what led to the resilience of the real estate market in an unprecedented situation  facing the COVID-19 pandemic. Last year, we discussed the activity of the housing market, which has not been seen since the market was heated before the financial crisis. Well, today we are recording more and more signs of a slowdown in real estate market activity. In the program, we have provided an opportunity to examine the signs in more detail  we will do so soon in the first part of the conference, which is devoted to the latest challenges, trends in the housing market, their causes and, indeed, possible consequences. Having mentioned the consequences, I would first of all like to draw attention to one sign of particular importance. I am referring to that undeniable fact that the rate of growth in house prices has overtaken wage increases. For the first time since the previous financial crisis, we recorded this change last year. This year, the trend is, unfortunately, the same. Which means that housing affordability is clearly declining  in the second year for acceleration... Colleagues Housing affordability is one of the main topics of this year's conference. Why exactly her? Because the topic of affordability is relevant to all of us  even those who do not think about buying or selling a home. Because housing is not only and not so much a real estate object, but above all a person's basic need  a roof over his head, a place to raise children, a sense of security and need for society. This may be an argument to stay in the country or an incentive to leave the country. The importance of housing affordability for man, the economy, society is confirmed not only by the analyses of academics, but also by living evidence  specific, I would say, resonant events in the life of society that happen when the roof overhead becomes too heavy a financial burden. Dear We will hear a number of presentations at the conference on housing affordability, and I have no doubt that a really interesting debate will boil over. But let's face it  it's important not only to discuss the topic. It is important that adequate action is finally taken. Therefore, in order to encourage a fruitful dialogue that will lead to the right decisions and actions, I will immediately mention a few measures focused on housing affordability. First of all, of course, the state's financial incentive for young families purchasing their first housing in the regions. The drive to improve housing affordability for young families is undoubtedly to be welcomed. But couldn't this help be more targeted, more targeted and, at the same time, more effective? It really could. Now we see that loans with incentive and support account for a large part of the total housing support flow in areas near major Lithuanian cities. But after all, the possibilities of buying housing in close proximity to large cities are fundamentally not in line with the objective of the incentive for the promotion of regional development. On the contrary, it contributes to the formation of imbalances in the districts adjacent to large cities. This shortcoming was highlighted by the Bank of Lithuania in its prepared conclusion on the state budget for 2023. I think the conference is a great format for discussing this tool more broadly. Nor should we forget about a properly calibrated real estate tax, which we must see as a tool that can contribute to a more sustainable development of the housing market in the long term. A properly calibrated tax would reduce incentives to buy a home for investment purposes and smooth out fluctuations in house prices. I therefore very much hope that we will soon be able to resume the debate on the review of the tax at political level. One can also mention the effective requirements for housing development. During the pandemic, we saw that the supply of housing did not keep up with the increase in demand, which significantly contributed to the acceleration of price growth and poorer affordability. It is therefore important to find a balance between the impact of development requirements on housing supply and the quality of housing must be assessed objectively, in accordance with the principle of a cost-benefit analysis. Colleagues housing affordability is a crucial issue that affects society now and will continue to function for decades to come. However, it is equally important to see, understand and react to what is happening in the market today. As I have already alluded to, we are seeing more and more signs that the activity of the housing market is slowing down. According to the data of the Centre of Registers, in the first three quarters of this year, eighth fewer housing purchase and sale transactions were registered in Lithuania than in the same period last year. The slowdown is particularly pronounced in the primary market for new apartments. The number of tentative contracts being terminated has increased. In other words, the tide seems obvious. Obviously, if we compare with the historical heights we saw a year ago. However, I will point out that even those reduced numbers are almost identical to the pre-pandemic 2019 figures, which we then also classified as historic highs. Therefore, in recent times, in the downward curves, perhaps, we should not see coolness or slump, but simply a normalization of the market, or, more simply, a return to normal. Prices. Despite the drop in sales, house prices continue to rise rapidly and supply remains limited, especially in the primary market. This is influenced by an increase in construction prices by about a fifth per year, which, it is true, has been stabilizing recently. There are naturally a few questions  how sustainable is the upward trend in prices? What is their likely further development? In conditions of global uncertainty, unfortunately, certainty does not exist. The activity of the housing market and its development in a broad sense is determined by a number of factors. First of all, the general state of the economy. The data evaluated in September showed that economic growth is slowing down  we forecast that this year Lithuania's economy will grow by 2.1 per cent, while next year  by only 0.9 per cent. The slowdown in economic growth and the ensuing consequences, plus an intolerably high inflation rate of 22% is a combination that makes it difficult for residents to save on housing. What's more, even those who would be able to afford it are forced to measure nine times before making such a large purchase. In order to contain the aforementioned high inflation, the world's central banks normalize monetary policy and raise interest rates. Higher interest rates and, at the same time, higher loan instalments will also cool the Lithuanian housing market, which has heated up during the pandemic, since the majority  even about 90 per cent  of housing loans are granted with variable interest rates. Abroad, we are already seeing the impact of higher interest rates and a slowdown in economic growth on housing markets that have become much hot during the pandemic and even before it, where there have been greater imbalances and the population is more indebted. In Sweden, for example, house prices have already fallen by more than a tenth compared to former historical highs. Across the Atlantic  in the U.S. and Canada  house prices are already recorded falling. It is not inconceivable that the cooling of house price increases will not bypass us either. Surveys of the Bank of Lithuania show that almost three quarters of households no longer expect house price growth in the coming years. The number of real estate professionals is also growing, who expect a more restrained and at the same time more sustainable, more fundamentally consistent with the growth of housing prices or a slight decrease in prices in major Lithuanian cities. Colleagues I understand that the shifts that I have mentioned and are being observed by yourself may seem like clouds accumulating on the horizon of the housing market, which are also thickened by the context of general uncertainty and the memories of 2008-2009. I am therefore pleased to have reason to say with confidence that the situation today is completely different. Why? Because, firstly, we have learned the lessons of the financial crisis in a really responsible way. Secondly, we not only learned, but also applied them in practice to prevent any "deja vu". The Bank of Lithuania's macroprudential measures, including the Responsible Lending Regulations, which came into force after the financial crisis, ensure the financial sustainability of borrowers and credit institutions. The down payment requirement increases banks' resilience to the risk of a decrease in loan collateral values. When granting a home loan, one is convinced of the possibility of residents to repay the loan, the possible increase in loan payments is also taken into account, which is especially true today. These measures have made it possible to ensure sustainable and safe growth of the debt of the population  the ratio of the debt of Lithuanian households to gross domestic product is lower than in the times of the financial crisis and one of the lowest in the European Union. This year, several additional measures established by the Bank of Lithuania to ensure the sustainability of the housing market came into force. I will not name them all, but to summarise them: yes, today we are facing the challenges of a period of uncertainty. But we're entering this, let's say, difficult obstacle course with financial sustainability and better prepared than ever before. Dear As it has become commonplace to say over the past few years, we are living in interesting times full of challenges and opportunities. Therefore, I am glad that you are interested in the real estate market, the processes taking place in it, you monitor and evaluate the latest trends. At the beginning of the conference, I hope that by discussing not only the current situation and risks of the real estate market, but at the same time we will look for and find effective solutions to mitigate these risks. I invite everyone to openly share their thoughts and insights! Thank you for your attention and  working and meaningful days! Financial Stability, Real Estate

Title: Speech by G. imkus at the presentation event of the collector coin dedicated to ukraine's struggle for freedom
text: Speech by G. simkus at the presentation event of the collector coin dedicated to ukraine's struggle for freedom For media Speeches, interviews, presentations RSS News subscription Print 2022-12-06 Speech by Gediminas simkus, Chairman of the Board of the Bank of Lithuania, at the event of the presentation of the collector coin dedicated to Ukraine's struggle for freedom. Your Excellency President of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, Honourable Members of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, Dear Ambassador, 1 of 1 Dear I bow my head to the Ukrainian people who are fighting for freedom, for the future of children, loved ones, the whole country and the whole of Europe. This struggle is important for every person in Lithuania who understands the feeling of desire for freedom, who remembers the history and suffering caused by the aggressor of the country  to everyone who loves his Homeland. Ukraine is not alone in this war. Lithuania as a state, its citizens, Lithuanian institutions, organizations support Ukraine's struggle for freedom. The 10 euro collector silver coin issued by the Bank of Lithuania for the struggle for freedom of Ukraine is exceptional. In the history of the Bank of Lithuania, this is the first such coin, one of the main goals of which is the collection of funds  70 euros from each purchased coin travels to assistance to Ukraine Although the coin will be issued only tomorrow, at the moment Lithuanian and foreign residents and companies have already bought about 60% of the coin circulation, which means that already about 215 thousand coins have been sold. the donated euros will be transferred to an account opened by the National Bank of Ukraine for the collection of humanitarian aid. When all the coins are purchased, the amount collected will reach one third of a million euros. The Bank of Lithuania and the National Bank of Ukraine have long-standing ties, friendly collegiate relations, which this wartime has only strengthened. It is not for nothing that our proverb says: you will know a friend in misfortune. At the beginning of the war, the Bank of Lithuania handed over an armored truck loaded with bulletproof vests and helmets to the National Bank of Ukraine for humanitarian purposes. On our website, we have promptly created a constantly updated information section for Ukrainians arriving in Lithuania, which contains important information about financial services. According to the agreement of the Bank of Lithuania with the National Bank of Ukraine, Ukrainian citizens fleeing the war were exchanged hryvnias for euros at siauli bankas. The trade union of our servants transferred funds to the organization Blue/Yellow, and our servants donated personally to colleagues from the Central Bank of Ukraine who suffered from the war. And we don't plan to stop. At the beginning of next year, we will issue a 2-euro commemorative coin called "Together with the Ukraine". The funds raised for it will also go to support Ukraine. At the same time, it will also be a circulation coin and will be used as a means of payment throughout the euro area, sending an important message to the whole of Europe. Dear today, a collectible coin is presented  not only 23.30 grams of silver, not only an opportunity to donate, but also an honor and commemoration of the heroic struggle of Ukrainians for freedom. This is both a numismatic value and a work of art that testifies to the historical events of today. I firmly believe that this coin will have a lasting value and will be important in the future, when Ukraine defend their freedom and thrive in the family of democratic and independent European states. It is symbolic that we are presenting this coin dedicated to ukraine's struggle for freedom today  the Day of the Armed Forces of Ukraine! It is the armed forces of Ukraine that are currently defending not only Ukraine, but also the whole of Europe, from barbaric attacks. Strength and fortitude for you! Dear in conclusion, I would like to congratulate and thank the artist Svitlana Matvieienko, who created the design of the coin, who, in a tiny piece of silver, was able to so sensitively fit the essence of the Ukrainian struggle for freedom and convey it to us in the language of symbols. At the same time, she shows both Lithuanian Vytis and Ukrainian Trisakis. Therefore, this coin also recalls the common roots of the history of Lithuania and Ukraine, as well as long-standing and current cooperation. Dyakuyu, Svitlano! I also thank all those who contributed to the creation and issuance of the coin: the team of the Bank of Lithuania, the Lithuanian Mint that minted the coins, the Embassy of Ukraine in Lithuania, with whom we are presenting the coin together, the Lithuanian Embassy in Ukraine, which advised us on various issues. And most of all, thank you to all those who buy a coin and thus contribute to helping Ukraine. Ukrainian Slava!
